name: Original Practice Test 3
source: Original LSAT-style questions written for LSAT Trainer (harder than the real test). Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Coach Varela has proposed shortening matches in the Ridgefield youth soccer league from sixty minutes to fifty in order to reduce player injuries. Admittedly, shorter matches would mean less total time on the field. Her proposal is nonetheless unlikely to achieve its aim. League records show that the large majority of injuries occur within the first twenty minutes of play, when players' muscles are not yet fully warmed up, and a shorter match would trim time only from the end of play. So the change would leave untouched the very period in which most injuries occur.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Most injuries in the Ridgefield league occur within the first twenty minutes of play, before players are fully warmed up.
Reducing the length of matches is not likely to bring about a meaningful reduction in injuries in the Ridgefield league.
The Ridgefield league should adopt measures to ensure that players are warmed up before play begins.
Shortening matches would leave untouched the period of play in which most injuries in the Ridgefield league occur.
Shorter matches would reduce the total amount of time that Ridgefield players spend on the field.
questions.explanation: The argument's main point is that the proposal is unlikely to achieve its aim of reducing injuries (B). D is the tempting trap: it appears in the last sentence, but it is an intermediate conclusion offered in support of B. A is a premise, E is a concession, and C is never asserted.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Coach Varela's plan to shorten matches is unlikely to achieve its aim of reducing injuries.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most injuries happen in the first twenty minutes, before players are warmed up; a shorter match only trims time from the end; so the change leaves the high-injury period untouched.

breakdown.analysis: Find the claim everything else is working to prove. The records support 'the change leaves the danger period untouched,' and that in turn supports 'the proposal won't achieve its aim.' The word 'nonetheless' flags the main point, right after the concession. Watch out: the last sentence starts with 'So,' but it's a stepping stone, not the destination. Ask yourself: why does the author care that the danger period is untouched? Because it means the plan won't cut injuries.

choices.note: This is a premise: the league-records fact that supports everything else. Facts like this are the reasons, not the point.
CORRECT. This restates 'her proposal is nonetheless unlikely to achieve its aim,' with the aim (reducing injuries) filled in. Every other claim in the passage is there to support it.

Never said. The author doesn't recommend any alternative measures. Warm-ups are mentioned only to explain why early injuries happen. Don't pick a conclusion the author would maybe like; pick the one the author actually argued for.

This is the trap. It's the last sentence and it starts with 'So,' which makes it look like the conclusion. But it's an intermediate conclusion: it exists to show that the proposal won't work. Lesson: 'so' marks a conclusion, but not always the main one. Ask what that claim is supporting.
This is the concession ('Admittedly, shorter matches would mean less total time on the field'). The author grants it and then argues the other way. A concession is never the main conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Marrow County election officials replaced the county's ballot with a redesigned version featuring larger type and simplified marking instructions. In the election that followed, the proportion of ballots rejected because they were improperly marked fell from 3 percent to under 1 percent. Clearly, then, the redesign must be responsible for this decline in rejected ballots.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on a comparison between elections that were held in different jurisdictions
treats one feature of the redesign as though it were the only feature that changed
draws a conclusion about all voters from a sample of ballots that may be unrepresentative
overlooks the possibility that some other difference between the two elections brought about the decline
takes for granted that improper marking is the only reason a ballot can be rejected
questions.explanation: The argument infers causation simply because the decline followed the redesign, ignoring other changes (different ballot length, voter outreach, a different electorate) that could explain it, so D is correct. E is tempting, but the argument concerns only ballots rejected for improper marking and makes no assumption about other grounds for rejection. A is inaccurate because both elections were in Marrow County.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ballot redesign caused the decline in ballots rejected for improper marking.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the redesign, the rejection rate for improperly marked ballots fell from 3% to under 1%.

breakdown.analysis: Classic correlation-to-causation flaw. One thing changed, then the rejection rate dropped, so the author says the change did it. But lots could differ between two elections: a shorter ballot, a voter education campaign, new poll workers, a different set of voters. It's like saying: I started wearing my lucky socks and my team won, so the socks won the game. Prephrase: the argument ignores other possible causes of the decline.

choices.note: Factually wrong about the argument. Both elections were in Marrow County. There's no cross-jurisdiction comparison.
choices.example: Example of flaw: City A's new traffic lights cut accidents by 20%, while City B, which kept old lights, saw no drop, so the lights work. (Different cities may differ in many ways.)

choices.note: Doesn't describe the argument. The author credits 'the redesign' as a whole: larger type and simpler instructions together. The author never singles out one feature.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The new menu added photos and cut prices, and sales rose. So the photos must be the only thing that changed and they drove the increase.

choices.note: No sampling issue here. The argument talks about the proportion of all ballots rejected, and its conclusion is about the cause of a decline, not about all voters' traits.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Of the twenty voters I asked at the country club, most support lower taxes, so most voters in the county support lower taxes.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument assumes that because the decline came after the redesign, the redesign caused it. It never rules out other differences between the two elections, like a shorter ballot or a voter outreach campaign. That's exactly the gap.

Tempting, but the argument only talks about ballots rejected because they were improperly marked. It never needs or assumes that improper marking is the only ground for rejection. Other reasons for rejection are simply outside its scope.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This ballot was rejected, and it wasn't improperly marked, so it must have been rejected by mistake. (Assumes improper marking is the only valid reason.)

questions.stimulus: The leaves of the coastal shrub Fenwick's sage are covered with fine hairs. Botanist Ilse Moravec hypothesizes that these hairs help the plant conserve water by trapping a layer of humid air against the leaf surface, thereby slowing evaporation. In support of her hypothesis, she notes that Fenwick's sage plants growing on dry, exposed bluffs have considerably denser leaf hairs than do plants of the same species growing in sheltered, moist ravines.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: When the hairs were removed from leaves of Fenwick's sage, those leaves lost water significantly faster than comparable leaves whose hairs were left intact.
Several other coastal shrubs whose leaves lack hairs grow abundantly on the same dry, exposed bluffs as Fenwick's sage.
Leaf hairs on Fenwick's sage reflect a substantial portion of incoming sunlight, keeping the leaf surface cooler than it would otherwise be.
Fenwick's sage plants on exposed bluffs receive substantially more direct sunlight than do those growing in ravines.
Fenwick's sage grows more slowly in moist ravines than it does on dry, exposed bluffs.
questions.explanation: A directly tests the hypothesized function: removing the hairs speeds water loss, as the hypothesis predicts. C is the main trap: a cooler leaf might lose less water, but C points to a different mechanism (reflecting sunlight) and so offers a rival account of why bluff plants have denser hairs, rather than supporting the humid-air hypothesis. D likewise suggests sun protection as the reason for denser hairs, and B and E do not bear on the hairs' function.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Hypothesis) The leaf hairs of Fenwick's sage help it conserve water by trapping humid air against the leaf and slowing evaporation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Plants on dry, exposed bluffs have denser leaf hairs than plants of the same species in sheltered, moist ravines.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence is only a correlation: drier spot, denser hairs. That fits the water hypothesis, but it fits other stories too, like the hairs protecting against sun or wind on the exposed bluffs. The best strengthener tests the specific mechanism directly. Think of it like testing whether a coat keeps you warm: don't just notice people in cold places wear thicker coats; take the coat off and see if they get colder.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the experiment. Take the hairs off and the leaves lose water faster. That's exactly what the water-conservation hypothesis predicts, and it shows the hairs actually do slow water loss rather than just happening to be denser in dry places.

Irrelevant to the hairs' function. Other shrubs surviving without hairs tells us nothing about what the hairs do on this plant. If anything it hints that hairs aren't needed on the bluffs, which nudges the wrong way.

The main trap. A cooler leaf might lose less water, so this feels supportive. But it gives a different job for the hairs: reflecting sunlight. That's a rival explanation for why bluff plants have denser hairs, not support for the humid-air mechanism. The LSAT is ultra specific: the hypothesis is about trapping humid air, not shading.

This helps a competing explanation. If bluff plants get more sun, the denser hairs might be sun protection, not water protection. That weakens the link between hair density and the humid-air hypothesis.
Growth rate doesn't tell us what the hairs do. Even if bluff plants grow faster, that says nothing about whether the hairs slow evaporation.

questions.stimulus: Every space heater sold by Halvorsen Appliances has passed the industry's tip-over test, and any heater that passes the tip-over test is equipped with an automatic shutoff switch. Several heaters sold by Halvorsen were recalled last year following customer complaints. However, according to the industry safety board, no heater that was equipped with both an automatic shutoff switch and an overheat sensor was recalled last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every heater equipped with an automatic shutoff switch has passed the tip-over test.
No heater sold by Halvorsen Appliances is equipped with an overheat sensor.
Some heaters that have passed the tip-over test were not sold by Halvorsen Appliances.
Every heater that was recalled last year was sold by Halvorsen Appliances.
At least one heater sold by Halvorsen Appliances lacks an overheat sensor.
questions.explanation: Each recalled Halvorsen heater passed the tip-over test and so has a shutoff switch; since no recalled heater had both a switch and an overheat sensor, those recalled heaters must lack an overheat sensor, so E must be true. B is too strong: only the recalled heaters must lack the sensor. A reverses the stated conditional, and C and D go beyond the information given.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Halvorsen heater → passed tip-over test; 2. Passed tip-over test → automatic shutoff switch; 3. Several Halvorsen heaters were recalled last year; 4. No heater with BOTH a shutoff switch AND an overheat sensor was recalled last year.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Halvorsen → passed tip-over → shutoff switch. So every Halvorsen heater has a shutoff switch. Fact 4 says: recalled → NOT (switch AND sensor), which means recalled → no switch OR no sensor. The recalled Halvorsen heaters have a switch, so they must have no sensor. Several recalled Halvorsen heaters exist, so at least one Halvorsen heater lacks an overheat sensor. Prephrase: some Halvorsen heater lacks an overheat sensor.

choices.note: Reversed conditional. We know tip-over test → switch, not switch → tip-over test. A heater could have a shutoff switch and never have taken the test. It's like saying: every dog is an animal, so every animal is a dog.
Too strong. Only the recalled Halvorsen heaters have to lack the sensor. The non-recalled ones could have both a switch and a sensor. Going from 'some' to 'none' is a classic overreach.
Nothing tells us about heaters from other makers. It's possible every heater that passed the test was sold by Halvorsen. Can't be proven.
The facts say several Halvorsen heaters were recalled, not that only Halvorsen heaters were recalled. Other brands' heaters could have been recalled too.

CORRECT. Recalled Halvorsen heaters passed the tip-over test, so they have a shutoff switch. No recalled heater had both a switch and a sensor, so those recalled heaters lack a sensor. Since several were recalled, at least one Halvorsen heater lacks an overheat sensor.

questions.stimulus:
Rhee: A scientific theory earns our confidence only by making predictions that could have turned out to be false and did not. A theory that merely accommodates data that had already been collected, however elegantly it does so, has not yet been tested at all.

Lindqvist: That standard is too strict. When a theory accounts for a large body of previously puzzling observations using fewer assumptions than its rivals, that achievement is itself a genuine test the theory has passed, even if the observations were known before the theory was formulated.
questions.stem: Rhee and Lindqvist disagree over whether
choices: a theory that makes successful predictions of new observations deserves some degree of confidence
simpler theories are generally more likely to be true than more complex ones
a theory's accounting for observations made before it was formulated can count as a test of that theory
most scientific theories are formulated only after the observations relevant to them have been made
a theory that makes even one false prediction should be abandoned
questions.explanation: Rhee says accommodating already collected data is no test at all, while Lindqvist says explaining previously known observations can be a genuine test, so they disagree about C. A is a point both would likely accept; Lindqvist does not deny that successful novel predictions earn confidence. Neither speaker addresses B, D, or E.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rhee: A theory earns confidence only by surviving risky predictions; accommodating data already collected isn't a test at all; Lindqvist: That's too strict; explaining lots of previously puzzling, already-known observations with fewer assumptions than rivals is itself a genuine test.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Find the claim they hit head-on: can explaining data you already had count as testing the theory? Rhee says no ('has not yet been tested at all'). Lindqvist says yes ('a genuine test the theory has passed, even if the observations were known before'). That's the issue. It's like two teachers arguing whether a student who explains last week's solved problems has been tested, or only one who solves new problems.

choices.note: Both would agree. Rhee says successful risky predictions are what earn confidence. Lindqvist never disputes that; he just says there's another way to pass a test too. Agreement isn't disagreement.

Neither speaker states this. Lindqvist praises theories that use fewer assumptions than rivals, but he doesn't claim simpler theories are generally more likely to be true, and Rhee says nothing about simplicity.

CORRECT. Rhee: accommodating already-collected data is no test at all. Lindqvist: accounting for previously known observations can be a genuine test. One says no, the other says yes. That's the disagreement.
Neither one makes a claim about how most theories are actually formulated. This is a historical/statistical claim outside the conversation.
Nobody discusses what to do after a false prediction. Rhee mentions predictions that could have been false, but neither speaker says a single failure means abandoning the theory.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, volunteers rated their mood after spending an hour in either a room painted pale blue or a room painted bright orange. On average, those who had been in the blue room reported calmer moods than those who had been in the orange room. The researchers concluded that pale blue surroundings tend to have a calming effect on people. But this conclusion is plainly mistaken. A painter I know has worked in a pale blue studio for years, and she is one of the most agitated people I have ever met.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it
choices: treats a single case as sufficient to refute a claim about a general tendency
attacks the researchers' character rather than the reasoning behind their conclusion
fails to consider that the volunteers' reports of their own moods may have been inaccurate
presupposes the truth of the very conclusion it is trying to establish
confuses a condition sufficient for calmness with a condition necessary for it
questions.explanation: The researchers claimed only that pale blue surroundings tend to calm people; one agitated painter cannot refute a claim about an average tendency, so A is correct. C is tempting because it names a real weakness of the study, but the arguer's reasoning does not depend on the accuracy of the mood reports; the arguer's error lies in the anecdotal counterexample.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The researchers' conclusion that pale blue surroundings tend to calm people is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A painter the author knows has worked in a pale blue studio for years and is very agitated.

breakdown.analysis: The researchers made a claim about a tendency: on average, blue rooms calm people. One agitated painter can't refute that. Tendencies allow exceptions. It's like arguing: my grandpa smoked his whole life and lived to 95, so smoking doesn't tend to shorten lives. Also, the painter might be even more agitated without the blue. Prephrase: the argument uses one anecdote to knock down a general tendency.

choices.note: CORRECT. The researchers said pale blue 'tends' to calm people. The author tries to refute that with one counterexample: a single agitated painter. One case can't disprove a general tendency.
The author never attacks the researchers as people. No comments about their motives, honesty, or competence. The criticism is about their conclusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The researchers' conclusion is wrong; after all, they're funded by a paint company.

choices.note: Tempting because it's a real weakness of the study. But the question asks about the author's reasoning, and the author doesn't rely on the mood reports at all. The author's mistake is the anecdote, not ignoring self-report problems.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Everyone in the survey said they felt happier after the vacation, so the vacation made them happier. (Ignores that self-reports might be inaccurate.)

choices.note: No circular reasoning. The premise (an agitated painter in a blue studio) is different from the conclusion (the study's claim is wrong).
choices.example: Example of flaw: Blue rooms don't calm people, because the color blue has no calming effect.

choices.note: There's no sufficient/necessary confusion. The author doesn't argue that blue is required for calm or that calm requires blue. The error is generalizing from one case.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Blue rooms calm people. Maria is calm, so she must have been in a blue room.

questions.stimulus: The cod population of Tessaly Bay has fallen sharply over the past decade. To reverse this decline, regulators plan to increase the minimum mesh size of trawl nets used in the bay. The larger mesh will allow most juvenile cod that encounter the nets to pass through them unharmed. Since an increase in the number of juvenile cod that survive to reproductive age will boost the population, the new regulation will help reverse the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The decline in Tessaly Bay's cod population was caused primarily by trawling.
Most juvenile cod that pass through the larger mesh will survive to reproductive age.
No other regulation would reverse the decline more quickly than the new mesh requirement.
At present, a significant number of juvenile cod in Tessaly Bay are caught in trawl nets.
Fishers in Tessaly Bay will not object to the new mesh size requirement.
questions.explanation: If few juvenile cod are currently caught in trawl nets, letting them pass through would not increase juvenile survival, and the argument collapses; so it requires D. A is attractive but too strong: the regulation could help even if trawling were only one of several causes of the decline. B is also too strong, since the argument needs only that more juveniles survive than before, not that most of those escaping do.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The larger-mesh regulation will help reverse the decline of the Tessaly Bay cod population.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Larger mesh lets most juvenile cod that encounter the nets pass through unharmed; more juveniles surviving to reproductive age will boost the population.

breakdown.analysis: The plan only helps if the nets are currently catching juvenile cod. If almost no juveniles get caught now, letting them slip through changes nothing, and juvenile survival doesn't go up. It's like installing a bigger hole in a fence to let deer through when no deer were getting stuck in the first place. Prephrase: a meaningful number of juveniles are currently being caught. Use the negation test: if negating the answer wrecks the argument, it's the assumption.

choices.note: Too strong. Negating it, the decline was not caused primarily by trawling. The argument survives: trawling could still be one cause, and reducing juvenile catch could still help. The argument only says the rule will help reverse the decline, not that it fixes the main cause.
choices.negation: The decline was not caused primarily by trawling.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument only needs more juveniles to survive than before, not most of the ones that escape. Negate it: fewer than half of escaping juveniles survive to reproductive age. Some still survive who wouldn't have, so the population could still get a boost. Argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most juvenile cod that pass through the larger mesh will survive to reproductive age.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. The argument says this rule will help, not that it's the fastest fix. Negate it: some other rule would work faster. This rule could still help. No damage.
choices.negation: Some other regulation would reverse the decline more quickly than the new mesh requirement.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: at present, no significant number of juvenile cod are caught in trawl nets. Then letting them pass through doesn't save any meaningful number, juvenile survival doesn't go up, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: At present, no significant number of juvenile cod in Tessaly Bay are caught in trawl nets.

choices.note: Objections don't matter unless they stop the rule from working. Negate it: fishers will object. They can complain all day and the rule can still help. Argument survives.
choices.negation: Fishers in Tessaly Bay will object to the new mesh size requirement.

questions.stimulus: Building codes in the city of Calder require that buildings constructed after 1990 have far more insulation than was required for buildings constructed earlier. Yet a survey of Calder's office buildings found that, on average, those constructed after 1990 use more energy per square meter for heating and cooling than do those constructed before 1990.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The cost of insulation materials has declined substantially since 1990.
Calder office buildings constructed after 1990 typically have extensive glass facades, which let far more heat pass through than do the masonry walls typical of older buildings.
Some Calder office buildings constructed before 1990 have since been retrofitted with additional insulation.
Residential buildings in Calder constructed after 1990 use less energy for heating than do older residential buildings.
Energy prices in Calder have risen steadily since 1990.
questions.explanation: B identifies a feature of the newer buildings that would increase heat transfer enough to outweigh their extra insulation, explaining their higher energy use. C is tempting, but retrofitting some older buildings would at most bring their insulation closer to that of newer ones; it would not explain why the newer buildings use more energy. D only deepens the puzzle, and A and E affect old and new buildings alike.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Post-1990 Calder buildings must have far more insulation, but post-1990 office buildings use more energy per square meter for heating and cooling than older ones.

breakdown.analysis: More insulation should mean less energy use, yet the newer buildings use more. We need something else about the newer buildings that leaks heat or adds load, enough to swamp the insulation advantage. It's like wearing a thicker sweater but leaving your jacket unzipped: the extra layer can't save you if the front is wide open. Prephrase: the newer buildings have some other feature that wastes far more energy.

choices.note: Cost doesn't explain energy use. Cheaper insulation might mean more insulation, which makes the puzzle worse, if anything.

CORRECT. Big glass facades let far more heat through than old masonry walls. That's a feature of newer buildings that can outweigh the extra insulation and explain why they use more energy despite better insulation.

Tempting, but it only narrows the insulation gap. Even if some older buildings caught up on insulation, that wouldn't explain why the newer buildings use more energy. At best it explains why they don't use much less.
Wrong group, and it deepens the puzzle. Newer residential buildings behave the way we'd expect, which makes the office buildings even more puzzling.
Prices hit old and new buildings alike, and the comparison is about energy used, not money spent. Doesn't explain a difference between the groups.

questions.stimulus: Sports analyst: Over the past five seasons, Northern League basketball players who wore the new Strata compression sleeves missed, on average, 30 percent fewer games due to injury than did players who did not wear them. This difference is too large to be a matter of chance. Clearly, then, wearing Strata sleeves substantially reduces a player's risk of injury.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Players who began wearing Strata sleeves had missed about as many games to injury in the preceding season as had players who never wore them.
Some players who wore Strata sleeves nonetheless missed many games due to injury.
Compression sleeves of various brands have been shown to increase blood flow to the muscles they cover.
Players who wore Strata sleeves played, on average, more minutes per game than did players who did not wear them.
Northern League trainers generally discouraged players with a history of recurring injuries from using any unproven equipment, including Strata sleeves.
questions.explanation: E weakens the argument by showing the comparison groups were unlike from the start: players prone to injury were steered away from the sleeves, so the sleeve wearers may have missed fewer games simply because they were less injury-prone. A is the main trap but points the wrong way: if wearers had injury records similar to non-wearers before adopting the sleeves, that rules out exactly this selection effect and strengthens the argument. D also strengthens it, since wearers had more exposure to injury yet missed fewer games.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Wearing Strata sleeves substantially reduces a player's risk of injury.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Over five seasons, players who wore Strata sleeves missed 30% fewer games to injury than non-wearers; the difference is too big to be chance.

breakdown.analysis: This is a comparison between groups that chose themselves. Ruling out chance doesn't rule out a third factor. Maybe the wearers were healthier players to begin with. It's like noting that people who buy gym memberships are fitter, and concluding the membership card makes you fit. Prephrase: something made the wearers less injury-prone from the start.

choices.note: The trap, and it points the wrong way. If wearers and non-wearers had similar injury records before the sleeves, that rules out the selection effect. That strengthens the argument.
Averages allow exceptions. Some wearers getting hurt is fully consistent with sleeves reducing risk overall.
This gives a possible mechanism (better blood flow), which, if anything, makes the causal claim more believable. It doesn't weaken.
Strengthens. Wearers were on the court more, so more exposed to injury, yet still missed fewer games. That makes the sleeves look even better.

CORRECT. Trainers steered injury-prone players away from the sleeves. So the wearers were a healthier group to begin with, and that alone could explain why they missed fewer games. The sleeves might do nothing.

questions.stimulus: Some election administrators argue that allowing voters to register on election day will overwhelm polling-place staff and lengthen lines. This concern is understandable but overstated. In the three states that most recently adopted same-day registration, average waiting times at polling places did not increase measurably in the first election after adoption. Admittedly, those states also hired additional poll workers for that election. But the number of workers they added was small relative to the number of same-day registrants, so the added staff cannot by itself account for the absence of longer lines.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that those states also hired additional poll workers for that election?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion.
It is offered as direct evidence that the administrators' concern is overstated.
It acknowledges a fact that might seem to undermine the argument's evidence, which the argument then contends does not do so.
It is a claim that the argument attempts to show is false.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the number of added workers was small.
questions.explanation: The hiring of additional workers is conceded ('Admittedly') because it could explain the absence of longer lines and so weaken the evidence; the argument then explains why it does not, matching C. D is the trap: the argument never disputes that the workers were hired, only that the hiring accounts for the result. The main conclusion is that the concern is overstated, so A is wrong.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Administrators' concern that same-day registration will overwhelm staff and lengthen lines is overstated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In three states that adopted it, waiting times didn't increase measurably; those states did add poll workers, but too few to account for the lack of longer lines.

breakdown.analysis: 'Admittedly' is the tell. The author concedes a fact that a critic could use: maybe lines stayed short only because extra workers were hired. Then the author answers it: the added staff was too small to explain the result. So the hiring claim is a potential objection to the evidence that the author raises and then defuses. It's like saying: sure, I studied with a tutor, but only for one hour, so the tutor can't explain my jump in scores.

choices.note: The main conclusion is that the administrators' concern is overstated. The hiring claim is a conceded fact, not the point.
Backwards. The hiring doesn't show the concern is overstated; it's a fact that could cut against the author's evidence. The direct evidence is the unchanged waiting times.

CORRECT. The author admits the states hired more workers, which might seem to explain away the short lines and so undermine the evidence. Then the author argues it doesn't, because the added workers were too few.
The trap. The author never claims the workers weren't hired; 'Admittedly' accepts it as true. What the author disputes is whether the hiring explains the result, not whether it happened.
Nothing supports 'the number was small' except a bare assertion. The hiring claim is what the 'small number' claim responds to, not evidence for it.

questions.stimulus: Conservation biologist: The orchid Dendra pallida, which is native to the Pellam Highlands, can germinate only in the presence of one particular species of soil fungus. Any plant whose germination depends on a single fungal species is vulnerable to soil disturbance unless its seeds can remain dormant for more than a decade, and no orchid native to the Pellam Highlands produces seeds that can remain dormant that long. Hence Dendra pallida should be included in the regional conservation registry.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: No plant species should be excluded from the regional conservation registry if it is vulnerable to soil disturbance.
Any plant whose germination depends on a single fungal species and whose seeds can remain dormant for more than a decade should be included in the registry.
Every plant species included in the regional conservation registry is vulnerable to soil disturbance.
Only plant species that are vulnerable to soil disturbance should be included in the regional conservation registry.
The seeds of Dendra pallida cannot remain dormant for more than a decade.
questions.explanation: The premises chain together to show that Dendra pallida depends on a single fungus and lacks long-dormant seeds, and so is vulnerable to soil disturbance. A, phrased negatively, says any vulnerable species should not be excluded, that is, should be included, which completes the argument. D is the main trap: it makes vulnerability necessary for inclusion, not sufficient, so it does not yield the conclusion. C reverses the needed conditional, B describes plants unlike Dendra pallida, and E merely restates something already derivable.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dendra pallida should be included in the regional conservation registry.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dendra pallida germinates only with one fungus species; single-fungus germination → vulnerable to soil disturbance unless seeds stay dormant 10+ years; no Pellam Highlands orchid has seeds that stay dormant that long.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain. Dendra pallida: single-fungus germination, and (being a Pellam orchid) no 10+ year dormancy. Single fungus AND no long dormancy → vulnerable to soil disturbance. So Dendra pallida is vulnerable. Conclusion: should be included. Missing link: vulnerable → should be included. Prephrase: any plant vulnerable to soil disturbance should be in the registry. Sufficient-assumption answers can be stronger than needed, but they must make the conclusion follow.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'No vulnerable species should be excluded' means vulnerable → should be included. The premises prove Dendra pallida is vulnerable, so it should be included. Chain complete: single fungus + no long dormancy → vulnerable → include.
Describes plants with seeds that do stay dormant 10+ years. Dendra pallida's seeds don't. So this rule never applies to it. Wrong group.

Reversed. This says in registry → vulnerable. We need vulnerable → should be in registry. Knowing every registered plant is vulnerable tells you nothing about whether a vulnerable plant belongs there.

The main trap. 'Only vulnerable species should be included' makes vulnerability necessary for inclusion: included → vulnerable. Meeting a necessary condition doesn't guarantee anything. Lots of vulnerable plants could still be left out under this rule.
Already derivable. Dendra pallida is a Pellam Highlands orchid, and no such orchid has seeds that stay dormant that long. Restating a premise doesn't bridge the gap to 'should be included.'

questions.stimulus: In an experiment, participants memorized a list of words while seated either in a quiet room or in a room filled with recorded café noise. A day later, each participant was tested for recall in one of the two rooms. Participants who were tested in the same room in which they had memorized the words recalled more words, on average, than participants who were tested in the other room. This was true both for those who had memorized the words in the quiet room and for those who had memorized them in the noisy room.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Quiet surroundings are better suited to memorization than noisy surroundings are.
People who study in noisy surroundings should always be tested in noisy surroundings.
Background noise has no effect on recall when learning and testing take place in the same room.
Most participants recalled more words when they were tested in the quiet room.
Whether the conditions of testing match the conditions of learning can affect how much learned material is recalled.
questions.explanation: Recall was better whenever the test room matched the learning room, regardless of which room it was, which strongly supports E. A and D compare the rooms themselves, which the results do not address. B is far too strong, and C claims an absence of any effect that the data cannot show.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Participants memorized words in a quiet room or a noisy café-sound room; 2. A day later they were tested in one of the two rooms; 3. Those tested in the same room where they learned recalled more on average; 4. This held both for quiet-room learners and noisy-room learners.

breakdown.analysis: The pattern is about matching, not about which room is better. Quiet-learn/quiet-test beat quiet-learn/noisy-test, and noisy-learn/noisy-test beat noisy-learn/quiet-test. So whether the test setting matches the learning setting affects recall. Prephrase: matching conditions helps recall. Stay modest: 'most strongly supported' answers that use soft words like 'can affect' are usually the winners.

choices.note: Compares the rooms themselves. The data only compares matched vs. mismatched conditions. We have no information on whether quiet-room learners did better overall.
Way too strong. 'Should always' is a sweeping recommendation from one experiment. Maybe other factors matter more in real life.
Claims no effect at all, which the data can't show. We only know matching helped; we don't know that noise level makes zero difference when rooms match. Noisy-noisy could still trail quiet-quiet.
No information about which test room produced more recall overall. Unsupported.
CORRECT. Matched learners beat mismatched learners in both directions. That's exactly evidence that matching conditions can affect recall. 'Can affect' is modest enough to be fully supported.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Some critics argue that because scientific theories have repeatedly been overturned in the past, we should expect our current theories to be overturned as well. But every theory that has been overturned was overturned by scientists applying the scientific method. So the history of overturned theories, far from undermining science, shows that the scientific method is reliable. We may therefore conclude that our current scientific theories are likely to be true.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that some theories may have been overturned by means other than the scientific method
moves from a claim about the reliability of a method for correcting theories to a conclusion about the truth of the theories that method currently supports
relies on the authority of scientists rather than on evidence about the theories themselves
treats the fact that past theories have been overturned as evidence that current theories will also be overturned
draws a conclusion that merely restates one of the premises offered in its support
questions.explanation: The premises show at most that the scientific method reliably corrects errors; that is compatible with current theories also being overturned later, so the argument illegitimately concludes they are likely true (B). D is a trap: that inference belongs to the critics, which the philosopher rejects rather than commits. A is wrong because the argument states as a premise that every overturned theory was overturned by the scientific method, and accepting a premise is not a flaw.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Our current scientific theories are likely to be true.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every overturned theory was overturned by scientists using the scientific method; so the history of overturned theories shows the method is reliable.

breakdown.analysis: The premises show at most that the scientific method is good at catching and correcting errors. That's a claim about the method, not about whether today's theories are right. A reliable correction process is perfectly consistent with today's theories getting overturned tomorrow. It's like saying: our editor always catches mistakes eventually, so this first draft is probably error-free. Prephrase: it jumps from 'the method reliably corrects theories' to 'current theories are true.'

choices.note: The author states as a premise that every overturned theory was overturned by the scientific method. Accepting a premise isn't a flaw; on the LSAT you take the premises as true.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All the burglaries in our town were solved by the police, so the police must be effective. (Ignores that some may have been solved by private investigators.)

choices.note: CORRECT. The premises establish, at most, that the method reliably corrects errors over time. The conclusion is about the truth of current theories, which the method might still overturn later. That's the jump.
The argument doesn't lean on scientists' authority. It reasons from the history of how theories were overturned.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The new diet works, because a famous scientist endorsed it.

choices.note: The trap. That inference is the critics' view, which the philosopher rejects. The philosopher doesn't commit it; he argues the opposite.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every past stock market boom ended in a crash, so this boom will surely end in a crash too.

choices.note: Not circular. The premise is about how past theories were overturned; the conclusion is about current theories being true. They're different claims, which is exactly why there's a gap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This medicine is effective because it works.

questions.stimulus: A manufacturer that learns of a hazard in one of its products is obligated to warn consumers promptly if the hazard could cause serious injury and consumers could not reasonably be expected to discover the hazard on their own. If either of these conditions is not met, the manufacturer may decide whether to issue a warning on the basis of other considerations.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Pinewood Furniture learned that the finish on one of its chairs can cause a mild, temporary rash, a hazard consumers could not detect in advance. So Pinewood was obligated to warn consumers promptly.

Marlo Housewares learned that the handle of one of its kettles can get hot enough to cause serious burns, a fact made evident before use by a prominent label and by steam that visibly vents beside the handle. So Marlo was obligated to warn consumers promptly.

Ostrander Ladders learned that rungs on one of its ladders can crack without any visible sign, risking serious falls. Since Ostrander had already stopped selling that ladder, it was not obligated to warn consumers.

Trevlan Tools learned that the blade guard on one of its saws can detach, risking severe cuts, and that the loosening cannot be detected without disassembling the saw. So Trevlan was obligated to warn consumers promptly.
Quella Toys learned that small magnets in one of its toys could cause serious internal injuries if swallowed, a hazard consumers could not detect. So Quella was obligated to recall the toy.
questions.explanation: In D the hazard could cause serious injury and cannot reasonably be discovered by consumers, so both conditions are met and the obligation to warn applies. E is the strongest trap: both conditions are met, but the principle requires only a prompt warning, not a recall. C is also tempting, but whether the ladder is still sold is irrelevant; both conditions are met, so a warning was obligatory. In A the hazard is not serious, and in B it is readily discoverable.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If a manufacturer learns of a hazard AND the hazard could cause serious injury AND consumers couldn't reasonably discover it themselves → the manufacturer must warn consumers promptly. If either condition fails → the manufacturer may decide on other grounds.

breakdown.analysis: Two boxes to check: serious injury, and not reasonably discoverable. Both checked → must warn promptly. That's the only obligation the rule creates. So the right answer has a serious, hidden hazard and concludes the company had to warn promptly. Not recall, not stop selling, not 'no obligation.' Principle-apply answers live or die on matching the exact outcome the rule names.

choices.note: Fails the first box. A mild, temporary rash isn't a serious injury. So the rule leaves Pinewood free to decide; it doesn't create an obligation to warn.
Fails the second box. A prominent label and visibly venting steam mean consumers could reasonably discover the hazard. So the rule doesn't require a warning here.

Tempting because it sounds sensible, but the rule doesn't care whether the product is still sold. Hidden cracks risking serious falls meet both conditions, so the rule says Ostrander was obligated to warn. This answer reaches the opposite outcome.

CORRECT. Severe cuts: serious injury. Loosening that can't be detected without taking the saw apart: not reasonably discoverable. Both conditions met → obligated to warn promptly. Exactly the rule's outcome.
The trap. Both conditions are met, but the rule only requires a prompt warning. It says nothing about a recall. The LSAT is ultra specific: the principle is about warning, not recalling.

questions.stimulus: To protect the declining population of salmon in the Arden River, the regional fisheries board closed the river's lower reaches to recreational fishing three years ago. Since then, the number of adult salmon returning to the Arden River to spawn has risen by 40 percent. The board's director concludes that the fishing closure is responsible for this increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether most recreational fishers in the region support the closure
whether the Arden River salmon population had been declining for more than a decade before the closure
whether the number of adult salmon returning to spawn in nearby rivers that remained open to fishing also rose over the same period
whether salmon are the species most sought by recreational fishers on the Arden River
whether the fisheries board intends to extend the closure to the river's upper reaches
questions.explanation: If salmon returns rose similarly in nearby rivers that stayed open, some regional factor rather than the closure probably explains the increase; if they did not, the director's conclusion gains support. So C is the most useful to know. B is tempting but concerns only the history of the decline, not what caused the recent increase; A, D, and E are irrelevant to the causal claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The closure of the Arden River's lower reaches to recreational fishing caused the 40% rise in returning adult salmon.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The closure happened three years ago; since then, returning salmon have risen 40%.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after causation. The question is whether something else, like better ocean conditions or a good year for salmon across the region, caused the rise. The cleanest check is a control group: nearby rivers that stayed open. If they also rose about 40%, the closure probably isn't the cause. If they didn't, the director looks right. It's like testing a new fertilizer: you'd want to know if your neighbor's unfertilized garden also boomed this year. Evaluate answers should give you a question whose two answers push the argument in opposite directions.

choices.note: Whether fishers like the closure says nothing about whether it worked. Popularity isn't causation.

Tempting, but it's about how long the decline lasted before the closure, not what caused the recent increase. Whether the decline ran 5 years or 15, we still don't know if the closure caused the rebound.

CORRECT. This is the control group. If open rivers also saw a jump, something regional likely explains it and the director is wrong. If they didn't, the closure looks like the cause. Either answer matters a lot.
Whether salmon are fishers' top target doesn't tell us whether the closure caused the rise. The fishers were catching salmon either way, or the closure wouldn't be framed as protecting them.
Future plans don't bear on what caused the past increase. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Race official: Every cyclist who receives a starting position in the Barrow Classic must both have registered by Friday and have completed at least two regional races this season. Ilona registered on Thursday, but she has completed only one regional race this season. Therefore, Ilona will not receive a starting position in the Barrow Classic.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Any building approved for the historic tax credit must both have been built before 1920 and retain its original facade. The Marston Building was built in 1905, but its facade was replaced in 1980. So the Marston Building will not be approved for the credit.
Every applicant hired by the firm must both hold a degree and have two years of experience. Petra holds a degree and has two years of experience. So Petra will be hired by the firm.

If a student both attends every lecture and completes every problem set, she will pass the course. Dara attended every lecture but did not complete every problem set. So Dara will not pass the course.
Only residents who have lived in the town for a year and own property there may vote on the levy. Gerald has voted on the levy. So Gerald must own property in the town.
Every successful bakery in the city both uses local flour and opens before 7 a.m. The Copper Loaf uses local flour and opens before 7 a.m. So the Copper Loaf is successful.
questions.explanation: The original states two necessary conditions for an outcome, shows that the subject meets one but fails the other, and validly concludes the outcome will not occur; A matches this exactly. C looks similar but treats the two conditions as sufficient, so concluding failure from missing one is a flawed denial of a sufficient condition. B and E wrongly infer the outcome from its necessary conditions, and D infers a condition from the outcome.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ilona will not receive a starting position in the Barrow Classic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Starting position → registered by Friday AND completed 2+ regional races; Ilona registered on time but completed only one race.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Outcome → X AND Y; subject has X but not Y; so subject won't get the outcome. (Valid: failing a necessary condition.)

breakdown.analysis: Map it with arrows. Start → registered AND 2 races. Contrapositive: not registered OR fewer than 2 races → no start. Ilona has fewer than 2 races, so no start. Valid. Find the answer that lists two required conditions, shows the subject meets one but misses the other, and concludes the outcome won't happen. Watch for answers where the conditions are sufficient, not necessary; that flips the logic.

choices.note: CORRECT. Credit → built before 1920 AND original facade. Marston meets the date but lost its facade. So no credit. Same two necessary conditions, one met, one failed, same valid conclusion. Even the 'but' structure matches.

Infers the outcome from its necessary conditions: Petra meets both requirements, so she'll be hired. That's invalid. Meeting the requirements doesn't guarantee the job. The original concludes the outcome won't happen; this one says it will.

Looks very close but the logic is different. Here, attending AND completing → pass, so the conditions are sufficient, not necessary. Missing one doesn't guarantee failure; Dara could pass some other way. The original is valid; this is a flawed denial of a sufficient condition.

Different direction. Voting → resident 1 year AND owns property; Gerald voted, so he owns property. That's valid, but it goes from the outcome to a condition. The original goes from a failed condition to no outcome.

Same flaw as B. Success → local flour AND early opening; Copper Loaf meets both, so it's successful. Meeting necessary conditions doesn't prove the outcome. Invalid, and it concludes a yes instead of a no.

questions.stimulus: Architectural historian: The nave of the cathedral at Vessan is about two meters wider at its western end than at its eastern end. Some scholars attribute this to deliberate design: the narrowing would make the nave appear longer to someone entering through the main doors at the west. More likely, however, the tapering resulted from measurement error. The nave was built over sixty years by successive crews, beginning at the eastern end, and builders of that era commonly laid out foundations section by section using ropes that stretched in humid weather.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Ropes used by builders of that era were often made of fibers that stretch less than most other fibers available at the time.
Several cathedrals built in the same era were deliberately designed to create optical illusions for visitors.
Careful measurements show that the nave of the Vessan cathedral narrows at a steady, uniform rate along its entire length from west to east.
When viewed from the western doors, the nave of the Vessan cathedral does appear noticeably longer than it actually is.
The width of the nave does not change gradually but shifts abruptly at several points that coincide with the boundaries between sections built by different crews.
questions.explanation: A deliberate optical design would produce a smooth taper, whereas abrupt shifts at the boundaries between crews' sections are just what section-by-section measurement error would produce, so E strengthens the historian's view. C is the subtlest trap: it looks like confirming evidence about the taper, but a steady, uniform narrowing is the signature of a planned design and therefore weakens the argument. D likewise supports the rival optical-illusion explanation, and A and B also tend to weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Vessan nave's tapering most likely resulted from measurement error, not deliberate design.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The nave was built over sixty years by successive crews, starting at the east end; builders then laid out foundations section by section with ropes that stretched in humid weather.

breakdown.analysis: Two rival stories, and each predicts a different shape. Deliberate design to make the nave look longer would give a smooth, even taper. Section-by-section rope error would give jumps and kinks wherever one crew's section met the next. So the best strengthener shows the width changing in a way only the error story predicts. It's like telling a hand-drawn line from a ruled one: the hand-drawn one wobbles where you lifted your pen.

choices.note: Weakens. If their ropes stretched less than other ropes, measurement error from stretching becomes less likely, which hurts the historian's explanation.
Weakens. If other cathedrals of the era were deliberately built to create illusions, the design explanation for Vessan looks more plausible.

The subtlest trap. It sounds like more data about the taper, but a steady, uniform narrowing along the entire length looks planned. That's the signature of deliberate design, so it weakens the error explanation.
Supports the rival view. If the nave really does look longer from the western doors, that's what the designers would have wanted, which helps the deliberate-design explanation.

CORRECT. Abrupt shifts lining up with the boundaries between different crews' sections are exactly what section-by-section measurement errors would produce. A planned optical effect would taper smoothly. This fits the historian's explanation and not the rival.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: A colleague claims that our finding, namely that people who are told a task is difficult persist at it longer than people who are told it is easy, is merely an artifact of our having used university students as participants. But if that were so, then repeating the experiment with participants drawn from a broader population should have eliminated the effect. We conducted exactly such a repetition, with participants recruited from community centers in three cities, and the effect was, if anything, stronger.
questions.stem: The researcher's argument proceeds by
choices: questioning the colleague's qualifications to evaluate the experiment
showing that the colleague's hypothesis implies a prediction that, when tested, turned out to be false
offering an alternative explanation of the finding that the colleague failed to consider
arguing that because the colleague's claim has not been proven, it must be false
showing that the colleague's hypothesis is inconsistent with the original finding it was proposed to explain
questions.explanation: The researcher derives a prediction from the colleague's hypothesis (a broader sample would eliminate the effect), tests it, and reports that it failed, which is B. E is the trap: the hypothesis conflicts with the result of the new replication, not with the original finding, which it was designed to explain away. The researcher does not offer a rival explanation of the finding (C) or attack the colleague's qualifications (A).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The colleague's claim that the finding is an artifact of using university students is wrong (implied).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If the colleague were right, repeating the study with a broader population would eliminate the effect; the researcher did that with community-center participants, and the effect was as strong or stronger.

breakdown.analysis: This is textbook hypothesis testing. Step 1: if the colleague's hypothesis were true, we'd expect X (the effect disappears with a broader sample). Step 2: test for X. Step 3: X didn't happen, so the hypothesis is in trouble. If H → P, and not P, then not H. It's like a friend saying your car only starts because it's warm out; you try it on a freezing morning and it starts right up.

choices.note: No personal attack. The researcher never questions the colleague's expertise; the response is all about the evidence.
choices.example: Example of method: My colleague's objection can be dismissed; he's never even run a psychology experiment.

choices.note: CORRECT. The researcher spells out what the colleague's hypothesis predicts (a broader sample would eliminate the effect), runs that test, and reports that the prediction failed. That's exactly B.
The researcher doesn't offer a new explanation of why people persist longer. She just defends the finding against the artifact claim.
choices.example: Example of method: My colleague says the effect is due to the student sample, but more likely it's because participants who were told the task was hard felt more pride in finishing it.

choices.note: The researcher doesn't argue from lack of proof. She points to positive evidence: the replication that went against the colleague's prediction.
choices.example: Example of method: No one has proven that the effect is an artifact, so it must not be one.

choices.note: The trap. The colleague's hypothesis was designed to explain away the original finding, so it's consistent with it. What it conflicts with is the result of the new replication.
choices.example: Example of method: My colleague says students persisted longer because they were rested, but the original data show they persisted longer even when tired.

questions.stimulus: Election commissioner: In our county, voters who cast ballots by mail must sign the return envelope, and that signature is compared with the one on file. In the last election, 2 percent of mail ballots here were rejected for signature mismatches, far more than in neighboring counties. Our staff are no less careful than staff elsewhere, so the high rejection rate is most likely due to the age of the signatures on file: a person's signature often changes over time, and unlike neighboring counties, we never ask voters to update their signatures.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The signatures of older voters change more over time than do those of younger voters.
Neighboring counties ask voters to update their signatures on file at least once a year.
Most voters in the commissioner's county cast their ballots by mail.
The proportion of mail ballots in the commissioner's county that were signed by someone other than the voter is not much greater than it is in neighboring counties.
If the county began asking voters to update their signatures, its rejection rate would fall below that of neighboring counties.
questions.explanation: If far more ballots in the county were actually signed by someone other than the voter, genuine mismatches rather than outdated signatures would explain the high rejection rate, so the argument requires D. B is too specific: the argument needs only that neighboring counties ask for updates, not how often. E is too strong; the argument does not require that the rate fall below that of neighboring counties.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The county's high signature-mismatch rejection rate is most likely due to old signatures on file.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The county rejected 2% of mail ballots for mismatches, far more than neighboring counties; county staff are no less careful; signatures change over time; unlike neighbors, the county never asks voters to update signatures.

breakdown.analysis: The commissioner explains the gap by outdated signatures and rules out one alternative (sloppy staff). But there's another obvious alternative: maybe the mismatches are real, because more ballots here were actually signed by someone else. The argument needs that not to be the case, or at least not to be a big difference. Prephrase: the county doesn't have a much higher rate of ballots genuinely signed by the wrong person. Negate each answer and see what breaks.

choices.note: Not needed. The argument is about signatures changing over time in general, not about older voters versus younger ones. Negate it and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: The signatures of older voters do not change more over time than those of younger voters.

choices.note: Too specific. The argument only needs neighboring counties to ask for updates at some point, not once a year. Negate it: they ask every three years. Still a difference from never asking; argument survives.
choices.negation: Some neighboring county does not ask voters to update their signatures at least once a year.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The rejection rate is a percentage of mail ballots, so it doesn't matter whether mail voters are a majority. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most voters in the commissioner's county cast their ballots by mail.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: far more ballots here were signed by someone other than the voter. Then the mismatches are genuine, and that, not outdated signatures, explains the high rate. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The proportion of mail ballots signed by someone other than the voter is much greater in the commissioner's county than in neighboring counties.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument says outdated signatures likely explain the gap; it doesn't need the county to end up below its neighbors after a fix. Negate it: updating would bring the rate down only to about the neighbors' level. That's perfectly consistent with the argument.
choices.negation: Even if the county began asking voters to update their signatures, its rejection rate would not fall below that of neighboring counties.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologist: Lobster harvests off the coast of Brennick Island have fallen by half over the past eight years. During the same period, the water temperature off the island has risen by about 1.5 degrees Celsius. Laboratory studies show that lobster larvae raised in water 1.5 degrees warmer than the island's historical average have markedly lower survival rates. So the warming of the island's waters is the main cause of the decline in the lobster harvest.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Lobster harvests have also declined in some regions where water temperatures have remained stable.
Adult lobsters can tolerate increases in water temperature considerably larger than 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Eight years ago, the number of boats licensed to harvest lobster off Brennick Island was cut in half, and the catch per boat has remained nearly constant since then.
Water temperatures off Brennick Island have fluctuated considerably over previous centuries.
Lobster larvae that survive to adulthood off Brennick Island grow somewhat faster in warmer water.
questions.explanation: If half the boats were removed and each boat's catch stayed constant, the halving of the harvest is fully explained by reduced fishing effort, not by fewer lobsters, which severely weakens the argument (C). A is attractive but shows only that something else can cause declines elsewhere; it says nothing about the cause at Brennick Island. B concerns adults, whereas the argument relies on larval survival.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Warming water is the main cause of the halving of the Brennick Island lobster harvest.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Harvests fell by half over eight years; water warmed 1.5°C over the same period; lab studies show larvae in water that much warmer have markedly lower survival.

breakdown.analysis: Watch the switch: the evidence is about lobster survival, but the conclusion is about the harvest. A harvest is how many lobsters people catch, which depends on how many lobsters there are AND how hard people fish. If fishing effort dropped, the harvest falls even with plenty of lobsters around. Prephrase: something else, like less fishing, explains the drop in harvest. It's like blaming a bad apple year for low sales when the store just cut its hours in half.

choices.note: Tempting, but it only shows that other things can cause declines in other places. It doesn't tell us what happened at Brennick Island. Warming can still be the main cause here.
Wrong group. The argument relies on larvae dying in warmer water. Adult tolerance doesn't touch that mechanism.
CORRECT. Half the boats, same catch per boat, means the total catch halves. The drop is fully explained by fewer boats, not fewer lobsters. Warming may not have mattered at all.
Past fluctuations are irrelevant to what caused the current drop. Lobsters may have suffered then too; it doesn't tell us anything about this decline.
Faster growth in survivors is a small upside, but it doesn't challenge the claim that fewer larvae survive. Doesn't weaken.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: The Kelby company's new electric bicycle battery has passed every safety test that regulators currently require. Nevertheless, Kelby should delay releasing it. Independent engineers have identified a plausible mechanism by which the battery could overheat during prolonged charging in hot weather, a condition that the required tests do not simulate, and Kelby has not yet investigated whether this overheating actually occurs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: Regulators should revise their required safety tests whenever engineers identify a hazard that those tests do not simulate.
A product that has passed all required safety tests should be presumed safe unless it has been shown to cause harm.
A company should delay releasing a product whenever it has confirmed that the product can overheat under conditions that required safety tests do not simulate.
A company should delay releasing a product only if it has confirmed that the product poses a hazard to consumers.
A company should not release a product while a credible potential hazard not addressed by required tests remains uninvestigated, even if the product meets all regulatory requirements.
questions.explanation: The advocate concludes that Kelby should delay release because a credible, untested hazard has not been investigated, despite regulatory compliance; E states exactly that principle. C is the closest trap, but it applies only once overheating has been confirmed, and Kelby has not confirmed anything, which is the advocate's very point. A addresses what regulators should do, not Kelby, and B and D point toward releasing the battery.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kelby should delay releasing its new battery.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The battery passed every required safety test; but engineers have found a plausible overheating mechanism in hot-weather charging, which the tests don't simulate; and Kelby hasn't investigated whether it actually happens.

breakdown.analysis: We need a rule that says: credible, untested hazard + not yet investigated → delay, even if all requirements are met. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, and its trigger has to match the facts. Here the key fact is that the hazard is only plausible and uninvestigated, not confirmed. It's like a mechanic saying: your car passed inspection, but I heard a weird noise from the brakes, so don't drive it on the highway until we check.

choices.note: Wrong actor. This tells regulators what to do, not Kelby. The conclusion is about Kelby delaying release.
Points the other way. If passing the tests means presumed safe until harm is shown, Kelby should release, not delay.
The closest trap. It triggers only once overheating is confirmed. Kelby hasn't confirmed anything; that's the advocate's whole point. So this rule doesn't apply to these facts.
Points the other way. Delay only if a hazard is confirmed, and here nothing is confirmed. Under this rule, Kelby isn't required to delay.

CORRECT. Credible potential hazard? Yes, a plausible mechanism. Not addressed by required tests? Yes. Uninvestigated? Yes. Meets regulations? Yes. Result: don't release yet. It matches every fact and gives exactly the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: In the alpine meadows of the Corvin range, the wildflower Lessia nivalis produces two kinds of flowers: showy flowers that must be pollinated by bumblebees, and small closed flowers that pollinate themselves. In years when bumblebees are scarce, Lessia plants produce a higher proportion of closed flowers. Researchers have found that Lessia plants fix the proportion of each flower type within the first two weeks after snowmelt, whereas bumblebees in the Corvin range do not emerge from hibernation until at least a month after snowmelt. Years of bumblebee scarcity in the range are reliably preceded by cold, late springs.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The proportion of closed flowers that a Lessia plant produces is probably determined by some cue other than the presence of bumblebees in the meadow that season.
In years when bumblebees are plentiful, Lessia plants in the Corvin range produce no closed flowers.
Lessia plants grown from the seeds of closed flowers produce fewer showy flowers than do other Lessia plants.
A cold, late spring causes bumblebee populations in the Corvin range to decline.
Showy Lessia flowers produce more seeds per flower than closed Lessia flowers do.
questions.explanation: Lessia fixes its flower proportions before any bumblebees have emerged, yet the proportions track bumblebee scarcity, so the plants must be responding to some other cue, such as spring conditions; this supports A. D is the main trap: the passage says only that cold, late springs reliably precede bumblebee scarcity, not that they cause it. B is too strong, and C and E are not addressed.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Lessia makes showy (bee-pollinated) and closed (self-pollinating) flowers; 2. In years of bee scarcity, plants make a higher share of closed flowers; 3. Plants fix the proportion within two weeks of snowmelt; 4. Bees don't emerge until at least a month after snowmelt; 5. Bee-scarce years are reliably preceded by cold, late springs.

breakdown.analysis: Here's the puzzle the facts set up: the plants lock in their flower mix before any bees are out, yet the mix tracks how scarce bees will be. So the plants can't be sensing bees directly. They must be using some other signal, and the cold-spring fact suggests what it might be. It's like a store stocking up on umbrellas before it rains; it's not reacting to rain, it's reading the forecast. Prephrase: something other than the bees themselves tells the plants what to do.

choices.note: CORRECT. The proportion is set weeks before bees emerge, so it can't be a response to bees in the meadow that season. Some other cue, like spring conditions, has to be doing the work. 'Probably' keeps it properly modest.
Too strong. We only know closed flowers are a higher proportion in bee-scarce years. Nothing says the plants make zero closed flowers when bees are plentiful.
Not addressed. The passage says nothing about what offspring of closed flowers do.
The main trap. The passage says cold springs reliably precede bee scarcity, not that they cause it. Preceding isn't causing. Both could result from something else, like a broader weather pattern.
Not addressed. Seed counts per flower are never mentioned.

questions.stimulus: City planner: No building in the Harrow district may exceed six stories unless it has received a variance from the zoning board. The board grants variances only to projects that include ground-floor retail space, and it grants no variance to any project that would reduce the number of on-street parking spaces. The proposed Linwood Tower, in the Harrow district, would exceed six stories and would include ground-floor retail space, but its loading dock would eliminate four on-street parking spaces. Therefore, the Linwood Tower will not be built as proposed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Most projects that the zoning board has denied a variance were later revised and then approved.
No building will be built as proposed if, as proposed, it could not lawfully be built in the Harrow district.
The zoning board grants a variance to every project that includes ground-floor retail space.
The developers of the Linwood Tower will not revise their plans in order to preserve the four parking spaces.
The Linwood Tower will not receive a variance from the zoning board.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that the tower as proposed exceeds six stories and cannot receive a variance (it would eliminate parking), so it could not lawfully be built as proposed; B links that to its not being built as proposed. E is a trap because it is already derivable from the premises and does not connect unlawfulness to what will be built. D is tempting, but the conclusion concerns the plan as proposed, so possible revisions are beside the point. C ignores the parking restriction and, in any case, does not close the gap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Linwood Tower will not be built as proposed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Harrow building over six stories → needs a variance; variance → includes ground-floor retail; reduces on-street parking → no variance; Linwood exceeds six stories, has retail, but eliminates four parking spaces.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Linwood eliminates parking → no variance. Over six stories without a variance → not allowed. So as proposed, Linwood can't lawfully be built. Conclusion: it won't be built as proposed. The gap is between 'can't lawfully be built' and 'won't be built.' Laws can be broken, after all. Needed link: can't lawfully be built as proposed → won't be built as proposed.

choices.note: Past revisions are irrelevant. The conclusion is about the plan as proposed. And a revised plan isn't the proposed one.

CORRECT. The premises show the tower as proposed couldn't be lawfully built in Harrow (over six stories, no variance possible). This answer says anything that couldn't lawfully be built as proposed won't be built as proposed. Chain complete.

Contradicts a premise and doesn't help. The board grants no variance to projects that cut parking, so not every retail project gets one. Even if it did, it would cut against the conclusion, not prove it.
Tempting, but revisions are beside the point. The conclusion is about what's built as proposed. Even if developers never revise, we still need a link from 'unlawful' to 'not built.'
