CORRECT. It has the whole conclusion: reduction stays ('remains an illuminating way'), its results depend on choices that 'could have been made otherwise,' so present a reduction as 'one hearing' rather than the work's structure.

Way too strong. The improvised-ornament traditions challenge one assumption about ornament. The author still calls reduction 'an illuminating way of describing one dimension of tonal coherence,' so coherence is real.

The trap. The author does say the circle is 'not necessarily vicious,' but then says it means the skeleton is 'partly a product of the analyst's prior expectations.' That's exactly why reductions should not be presented as revealing the structure. E flips the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A method is described, its origins are traced, and it is shown to have been superseded by a newer method.
Two competing methods are compared, and one is shown to be superior on the basis of two considerations.
A method is criticized on two grounds, those criticisms are shown to be unfounded, and the method is endorsed.
A method is described and its appeal acknowledged, two problems with it are raised, and a revised understanding of what it achieves is proposed.
A problem of interpretation is identified, a method for resolving it is introduced, and the method’s limitations are dismissed as minor.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes reduction and its appeal, the second and third raise the circularity and ornament problems, and the fourth proposes a more modest account of what reduction achieves, which is D. C is the trap because the method is retained, but the author never shows the criticisms to be unfounded; the revised account accepts them. E misdescribes the final paragraph, which takes the limitations seriously enough to change how reductions should be presented.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the passage's organization, paragraph by paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening move of each paragraph: P1 describes the method and its appeal; P2 'Yet the method rests on a decision ...'; P3 'A further difficulty ...'; P4 'None of this requires abandoning reduction.'

breakdown.analysis: Map it: P1, the method and why it's appealing. P2, problem one (circularity). P3, problem two (ornament as inessential). P4, keep the method but understand it more modestly. Prephrase: method described and praised, two problems raised, a more modest account of what it achieves proposed. On structure questions, check every piece of an answer against your map. One wrong verb ('dismissed', 'superseded', 'shown to be unfounded') kills it.

choices.note: Nothing traces the method's origins, and no newer method replaces it. The author keeps reduction.
Only one method is discussed. There's no competing method to compare.
The trap. The method is kept, but the criticisms aren't shown to be unfounded. The author accepts them and changes how reductions should be presented because of them.
CORRECT. P1 describes reduction and acknowledges its 'considerable' appeal; P2 and P3 raise two problems; P4 proposes a 'more modest account of what reduction achieves.'

Wrong on both ends. The passage starts by describing a method, not an interpretive problem, and the final paragraph takes the limits seriously enough to change practice. It doesn't dismiss them as minor.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following?
choices: Some notes’ classification as ornamental does not depend on the analyst’s expectations about the underlying progression.
Any reduction whose classifications rely on the underlying progression is for that reason invalid.
The skeleton an analyst uncovers is entirely a product of the analyst’s prior expectations.
In traditions where performers supplied the ornaments, reductive analysis cannot be applied at all.
In analysis, the pitches a composer notated should always take precedence over notes added by performers.
questions.explanation: The author says that in many cases the classification seems obvious—a brief stepwise note between chord tones is almost universally heard as decorative—and that analysts appeal to the underlying structure only in the cases that are not obvious; so some classifications do not rest on the analyst’s expectations about the progression, which is A. C is the key degree trap: the author says the skeleton is ‘partly’ such a product, not entirely. B contradicts ‘not necessarily vicious,’ and D overstates the third paragraph, which challenges a claim about ornament’s value without saying reduction is inapplicable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the author would most likely agree with. Watch for degree words.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2: 'In many cases the decision seems obvious ... But in many others it is not, and here analysts typically appeal to the very structure ...' and 'partly a product of the analyst's prior expectations.'

breakdown.analysis: The author splits notes into two groups. Obvious cases: a brief stepwise note between chord tones is 'almost universally heard as decorative.' Hard cases: here analysts lean on the underlying structure, which creates the circle. So the circle only affects the hard cases; the obvious ones don't depend on the analyst's expectations about the progression. Prephrase: some classifications don't depend on the analyst's view of the progression. The lesson: watch quantity words like 'partly', 'many', and 'entirely'. RC traps often push 'some' to 'all.'

choices.note: CORRECT. The author says that in many cases the classification 'seems obvious,' with a near-universal hearing of a stepwise passing note as decorative. The appeal to the underlying progression comes only in the cases that aren't obvious. So some classifications don't rest on expectations about the progression.
Contradicts the author. The circle is 'not necessarily vicious' and 'interpretation often proceeds by such mutual adjustment.' The author doesn't call such reductions invalid.
Degree trap. The author says 'partly a product,' not 'entirely.' One word, and it's out.
Overstates paragraph 3. That paragraph challenges the claim that ornament is inessential; it never says reduction can't be applied to such music.
Never said. The author doesn't rank composer's notes over performer's notes. If anything, paragraph 3 takes performers' ornaments seriously as a source of value.

questions.stem: The author’s stance toward the claim that a reduction reveals the structure of a musical work is best described as
choices: rejection of the claim together with rejection of reductive analysis as a method
acceptance of the claim, with reservations only about how analysts classify certain notes
agnosticism, on the ground that the considerations for and against the claim are evenly balanced
acceptance of the claim for music with fixed ornaments, but rejection of it for music with improvised ornaments
rejection of the claim as stated, combined with endorsement of a weaker claim about what reduction offers
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that ‘rather than revealing the structure of a work, a reduction offers one hearing of it,’ rejecting the strong claim while endorsing a weaker one, which is E. D is the most sophisticated trap: the ornament argument does apply specially to improvised traditions, but the circularity argument in the second paragraph applies to reduction generally, and the author’s conclusion is not limited to improvised music. A is wrong because the author says none of this requires abandoning reduction.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's stance on the specific claim that a reduction reveals a work's structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: 'Rather than revealing the structure of a work, a reduction offers one hearing of it.'

breakdown.analysis: The author rejects the strong claim ('revealing the structure') and replaces it with a weaker one ('one hearing,' shaped by choices). The method stays. Prephrase: reject the strong claim, accept a weaker one. And note the scope: the circularity problem in paragraph 2 applies to reduction generally, so the rejection isn't limited to any one kind of music.

choices.note: Half wrong. The author rejects the claim but keeps the method: 'None of this requires abandoning reduction.'
Wrong. The author doesn't accept the claim; the final paragraph explicitly replaces 'revealing the structure' with 'one hearing.'
The author isn't undecided. Paragraph 4 takes a clear position.

The most sophisticated trap. The ornament argument does apply to improvised traditions in particular. But the circularity argument in paragraph 2 applies to all reduction, and the conclusion in paragraph 4 is general. The author doesn't accept the claim for fixed-ornament music.

CORRECT. The author rejects 'reveals the structure' as stated and endorses the weaker claim that a reduction 'offers one hearing of it,' an 'illuminating way of describing one dimension of tonal coherence.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the circularity described in the second paragraph of the passage?
choices: A translator renders each of a poem’s idioms word for word, so that the finished translation is literally faithful to the original but awkward to read.
A historian assumes, without examining the matter, that the most recent document in an archive is the most reliable account of the event it describes.
An editor reconstructs an author’s original text by discarding readings judged to be copyists’ errors, and judges readings to be errors because they do not fit the text as reconstructed.
A critic evaluates a novel solely by comparing it with the other novels its author has written, ignoring the work of the author’s contemporaries.
A mapmaker leaves the minor roads off a regional map so that travelers can more easily see the major highways connecting its cities.
questions.explanation: In the passage, ornament is identified as what does not belong to the underlying progression, while the progression is identified by setting aside ornament; C has the same mutual dependence between the errors and the reconstructed text. E is the attractive trap because it involves simplifying by stripping away lesser details, but the mapmaker’s judgment of which roads are minor does not depend on the map that results, so there is no circle. B involves an unexamined assumption but not mutual dependence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Analogy question: find the case with the same circular structure as paragraph 2.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2: 'A note is classified as ornamental because it does not belong to the underlying progression, and the underlying progression is identified by setting aside the notes classified as ornamental.'

breakdown.analysis: Pattern: you identify X (ornaments) by checking them against Y (the progression), but you identify Y by removing X. Each depends on the other. Prephrase: something defined by what's left after removing things that were picked out by whether they fit what's left. Look for that two-way dependence, not just 'simplifying' or 'removing details.' It's like deciding who the 'real' members of a club are by who fits the club's culture, and defining the club's culture by what the real members do.

choices.note: No circle. A word-for-word translation trades readability for literal faithfulness; nothing depends on something that depends on it.
An unexamined assumption, not mutual dependence. The historian takes recency as a sign of reliability, but recency isn't defined by reliability.
CORRECT. Errors are discarded to reconstruct the text, and readings count as errors because they don't fit the reconstructed text. Same two-way dependence as ornaments and the progression.
A narrow comparison class, not a circle. Ignoring contemporaries is a different flaw.

The attractive trap, since the mapmaker strips away lesser details just as reduction strips away ornaments. But deciding a road is minor doesn't depend on the finished map, so there's no circle. Simplifying isn't the point; the mutual dependence is.

questions.stem: The author refers to performance traditions in which performers supplied the ornaments primarily in order to
choices: show that reductive analysis cannot explain how long movements are heard as coherent wholes
challenge the assumption that ornamentation is by its nature inessential to a musical work
provide an example of a case in which classifying a note as ornamental is obvious
argue that performers rather than composers should be regarded as the authors of tonal works
illustrate the circular reasoning described in the second paragraph
questions.explanation: Because listeners in those traditions judged performances chiefly by their ornamentation, treating ornament as inessential becomes a substantive and possibly mistaken claim about value, so the example challenges that assumption, as B says. E is the trap: the example follows the discussion of circularity, but the third paragraph introduces it as a ‘further difficulty,’ distinct from the circle. D overstates a point about where value lies into a claim about authorship.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function question: why does the author bring up traditions in which performers supplied the ornaments?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, which opens 'A further difficulty concerns the status of ornament itself' and ends by calling 'ornament inessential' a 'substantive claim about where the music's value lies.'

breakdown.analysis: Reduction treats ornament as inessential by definition. The author points to traditions where performers improvised ornaments and audiences judged performances mainly by them. In that music, calling ornament inessential is a value judgment the original listeners might have rejected. Prephrase: to challenge the assumption that ornament is inherently inessential. The phrase 'A further difficulty' tells you it's a new, separate problem, not more of the circle.

choices.note: Not the target. The author grants that reduction 'explains how a long movement can be heard as a coherent whole.' Paragraph 3 targets the ornament assumption, not that ability.

CORRECT. Paragraph 3's point is that in these traditions, calling ornament inessential 'is not a neutral analytic observation but a substantive claim about where the music's value lies.' That challenges the assumption that ornament is inessential by nature.
Backwards. The obvious-case example is in paragraph 2 (a stepwise note between chord tones). Paragraph 3 makes the status of ornament less obvious, not more.
Overreach. The point is about where the music's value lies, not who counts as the author of the work.
The trap. The example follows the circularity discussion, but it's introduced as 'a further difficulty,' a separate second problem about the value of ornament, not an illustration of the circle.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the author recommends that analysts who use reduction
choices: state their reasons for every note they classify as ornamental
give up the search for a skeleton that underlies an entire work
study the performance practices of a work’s original audiences before analyzing it
explain why they classified a note as they did wherever that classification is in dispute
present several alternative reductions of each work so that listeners can choose among them
questions.explanation: The final paragraph recommends stating, ‘wherever the classification of a note is contested, why they classified it as they did,’ which is D. A is the key trap: it uses the passage’s own idea but broadens it from contested classifications to every classification, which the author does not recommend and which the second paragraph’s point about obvious cases makes unnecessary. E is a plausible extension of ‘one hearing’ but is never recommended.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail question: what exactly does the author recommend analysts do?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: 'stating, wherever the classification of a note is contested, why they classified it as they did.'

breakdown.analysis: The recommendation is narrow: explain your classification wherever it's contested. Not everywhere, not multiple reductions, not giving up the skeleton. Prephrase: give reasons for contested classifications. The lesson: on detail questions, scope words matter. 'Every' is not 'wherever contested.'

choices.note: The key trap. It takes the author's idea and widens it from contested classifications to every one. The author limits it to disputed cases, and paragraph 2 says many cases are obvious, so explaining them all would be pointless.
Contradicts the author, who keeps the method: 'None of this requires abandoning reduction.' Looking for the skeleton is part of the method.
Not recommended. The original audiences come up in paragraph 3 as an argument about ornament's value, not as research analysts are told to do.
CORRECT. Almost word for word: 'stating, wherever the classification of a note is contested, why they classified it as they did.'
A plausible extension of 'one hearing,' but the author never recommends producing several reductions per work. Stick to what's stated.

questions.stimulus: Darvale’s housing council predicts that relaxing the city’s restrictions on backyard cottages will noticeably lower rents. This prediction is unlikely to be borne out. Admittedly, any new housing adds to supply, and added supply tends to restrain prices. But in cities that have already relaxed such restrictions, most new backyard cottages have been occupied by the owners’ relatives or listed as short-term vacation rentals. Units used in these ways do little to expand the stock of housing available to ordinary long-term renters.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Units occupied by owners’ relatives or used as vacation rentals do little to expand the housing available to long-term renters.
Adding to the supply of housing generally tends to restrain the prices of housing.
Relaxing Darvale’s restrictions on backyard cottages probably will not noticeably lower the city’s rents.
Darvale’s housing council should not relax the city’s restrictions on backyard cottages.
Most backyard cottages built in Darvale will be occupied by the owners’ relatives.
questions.explanation: The argument’s point is that the council’s prediction of lower rents is unlikely to come true, which C restates; everything else is offered in support of that. A is a premise supporting the conclusion, and B is a concession. D goes further than the argument, which never says the restrictions should stay in place.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The housing council's prediction that relaxing backyard-cottage restrictions will noticeably lower Darvale's rents is unlikely to come true.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In cities that relaxed such restrictions, most new cottages went to owners' relatives or short-term vacation rentals; units used that way do little to expand housing for ordinary long-term renters.

breakdown.analysis: The second sentence is the point: 'This prediction is unlikely to be borne out.' Then comes a concession ('Admittedly, new supply restrains prices'), then a 'But' with the evidence. Everything after sentence two is there to show why the rent prediction will probably fail. Find the answer that says relaxing the rules probably won't noticeably lower rents.

choices.note: This is the last premise: it explains why those cottage uses don't help long-term renters. It supports the conclusion; it isn't the conclusion.
This is the concession ('Admittedly...'). The author grants it and then argues the other way. A concession is never the main point.
CORRECT. This restates 'This prediction is unlikely to be borne out,' with the prediction filled in. Everything else in the passage supports it.

Goes too far. The author says the change won't noticeably lower rents, not that the council shouldn't do it. There could be other good reasons to relax the rules. Watch the jump from 'won't achieve X' to 'shouldn't do it.'

The author describes what happened in other cities, not a prediction about Darvale's cottages specifically, and it's 'relatives or vacation rentals,' not relatives alone. Too specific, and not the main point anyway.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: In a thorough survey of the Pellam Valley, we located 340 hives of the blue mason bee, and every one of them was within 200 meters of a stand of wild sage. Since wild sage grows in scattered stands across nearly the entire valley floor, the bees evidently have no trouble finding sites near it. Plainly, then, in the Pellam Valley it is the presence of wild sage that determines where blue mason bees build their hives.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to establish that the bees’ hive sites are any closer to wild sage than randomly chosen locations in the valley would be
draws a conclusion about the valley’s bees from a sample of hives that may not be representative of them
presupposes the truth of the very conclusion that it is attempting to establish
fails to consider that some hives may also have been located near plants other than wild sage
treats a condition that is necessary for hive building as though it were sufficient for it
questions.explanation: If sage stands are scattered across nearly the whole valley, almost any spot would lie within 200 meters of one, so the correlation reveals nothing about the bees’ choice of sites (A). B is the trap, but the survey was thorough and the conclusion is limited to the valley, so representativeness is not the problem. D is irrelevant, since nearness to other plants would not show that sage plays no role.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: In the Pellam Valley, the presence of wild sage determines where blue mason bees build their hives.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All 340 surveyed hives were within 200 meters of wild sage; wild sage grows in scattered stands across nearly the entire valley floor.

breakdown.analysis: The arguer undercuts their own evidence. If sage is almost everywhere, then almost any spot in the valley is within 200 meters of sage. So of course every hive is near sage; a hive dropped at random would be too. The correlation tells you nothing about choice. It's like noting that every house in town is within a mile of a Starbucks, in a town with a Starbucks on every corner, and concluding people pick homes based on coffee. Prephrase: no comparison to how close random spots would be.

choices.note: CORRECT. Since sage covers nearly the whole valley floor, random locations would also be near sage. Without showing hives are closer than chance would predict, the 100% match proves nothing about what drives site choice.
The trap. The survey was 'thorough' and the conclusion is limited to the Pellam Valley, so representativeness isn't the problem. The problem would remain even with a perfect sample.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We surveyed hives near the visitor center and found they were all near sage, so all the valley's hives must be near sage.

choices.note: Not circular. The premise is about where hives were found; the conclusion is about what determines where they're built. Different claims.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Sage determines where bees nest, because bees always choose their nesting sites according to where sage is.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Hives being near other plants too wouldn't show sage plays no role. It doesn't hit the real weakness: sage is everywhere.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every hive was near sage, so sage determines hive sites; never mind that every hive was also near clover and water.

choices.note: No necessary-sufficient confusion. The argument doesn't claim sage is required or that sage alone guarantees a hive.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Bees can only build hives where there's sage. This spot has sage, so the bees will build a hive here.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, forecasters at the Hollin weather station have noted that mornings with a southerly wind pattern known locally as the ‘lift’ are followed by afternoon thunderstorms far more often than are other mornings. The station’s lead meteorologist contends that the lift itself produces these storms: it pushes warm, moist air from the lowlands up the slopes of the nearby hills, where the air cools and its moisture condenses into storm clouds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the meteorologist’s argument?
choices: Afternoon thunderstorms also occur near Hollin on some days when the lift has not occurred that morning.
Weather stations in other regions rarely record a morning wind pattern resembling the lift.
The lift is most common in midsummer, when afternoon thunderstorms near Hollin are most common in general.
Forecasts issued by the Hollin station have become more accurate over the past decade.
On mornings when the lift occurs but the lowland air is unusually dry, afternoon thunderstorms near Hollin are rare.
questions.explanation: The meteorologist’s proposed mechanism depends on the lift carrying moist air uphill; if storms fail to follow the lift precisely when the lowland air is dry, that is just what the mechanism predicts (E). C weakens the argument by suggesting that season, not the lift, explains the correlation. A is compatible with the argument, since the lift need not be the only cause of storms.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lift itself produces the afternoon thunderstorms near Hollin.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lift mornings are followed by storms far more often than other mornings; proposed mechanism: the lift pushes warm, moist lowland air up the hills, where it cools and condenses into storm clouds.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence is a correlation plus a proposed mechanism. A great strengthener tests the mechanism: if storms come from the lift carrying moist air uphill, then when the lift blows but the air is dry, storms shouldn't follow. Confirming that prediction shows the mechanism really is what's at work. It's like testing whether a fan dries your laundry by blowing warm air: on days the air is cold, the laundry should stay damp.

choices.note: Compatible but not helpful. The meteorologist never said the lift is the only cause of storms. Storms on non-lift days don't strengthen the argument, and if anything they slightly dilute it.
Irrelevant. How rare the lift is elsewhere says nothing about whether it causes storms at Hollin.
Weakens. If the lift and storms both peak in midsummer, the season itself could explain the correlation. Classic third factor.
Forecast accuracy has nothing to do with what causes the storms.

CORRECT. The mechanism needs moist air. On lift mornings with dry lowland air, storms are rare, exactly what the mechanism predicts. That shows it's the lift moving moist air, not just the lift showing up alongside storms by coincidence.

questions.stimulus:
Imogen: The editors of the new anthology were right to exclude poems written in strict traditional forms. Most readers today find the sonnet and the villanelle stiff and artificial, and an anthology aimed at a general audience ought to feature work that its readers will find natural and engaging.

Teodor: An anthology that presents itself as a survey of contemporary poetry has an obligation to represent that poetry accurately, and several of the most admired poets working today write in strict forms. Whatever readers’ tastes may be, leaving such poems out misrepresents the field.
questions.stem: Imogen and Teodor disagree over whether
choices: most readers today find traditional poetic forms stiff and artificial
the anthology’s editors were justified in excluding poems written in strict traditional forms
several of the most admired contemporary poets write in strict forms
an anthology aimed at a general audience should include at least some poems in free verse
poems in strict traditional forms are more difficult to write than poems in free verse
questions.explanation: Imogen says the editors were right to exclude strict-form poems; Teodor says the exclusion misrepresents the field and so was a mistake (B). Teodor never disputes A (‘whatever readers’ tastes may be’), and Imogen never addresses C. Neither speaker discusses D or E.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Imogen: The editors were right to exclude strict-form poems, since most readers find them stiff and a general-audience anthology should feature engaging work; Teodor: A survey of contemporary poetry must represent the field accurately, and several top poets write in strict forms, so excluding them misrepresents the field.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Imogen: the exclusion was right. Teodor: the exclusion misrepresents the field, so it was wrong. That's the clash. Notice Teodor sidesteps reader taste ('whatever readers' tastes may be'), so they don't disagree about that. It's like two people arguing about whether the cafeteria should drop a dish: one says nobody eats it, the other says the menu should reflect the whole cuisine.

choices.note: Imogen says this, but Teodor sets it aside with 'whatever readers' tastes may be.' He doesn't deny it, so no disagreement.
CORRECT. Imogen says the editors were right to exclude the strict-form poems. Teodor says leaving them out misrepresents the field, so they weren't justified. Yes vs. no.
Teodor says this; Imogen never addresses it. One silent speaker means no disagreement you can prove.
Neither speaker discusses free verse or whether it should be included.
Neither speaker says anything about how hard strict forms are to write.

questions.stimulus: Each drug tested in the Corvane trial that reduced inflammation also raised blood pressure in at least some of the patients who took it. No drug tested in the trial was later approved for use in elderly patients unless it raised blood pressure in none of the patients who took it. Some of the drugs tested in the trial were later approved for use in elderly patients, and most of those drugs were also approved for use in children.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: None of the drugs tested in the trial that were approved for use in children reduced inflammation.
Some of the drugs tested in the trial that were approved for elderly patients reduced inflammation.
Most of the drugs tested in the trial that raised no patient’s blood pressure were approved for elderly patients.
At least one drug tested in the trial that was approved for use in children did not reduce inflammation.
At least one drug tested in the trial raised blood pressure in some of the patients who took it.
questions.explanation: Any drug approved for elderly patients raised no one’s blood pressure and therefore did not reduce inflammation; since some such drugs exist and most of them were approved for children, at least one child-approved drug did not reduce inflammation (D). A is the trap: drugs approved for children but not for elderly patients are unconstrained, so some could have reduced inflammation. E need not hold, since perhaps no drug reduced inflammation and none raised blood pressure.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Reduced inflammation → raised BP in some patients; 2. Approved for elderly → raised BP in no patients; 3. Some drugs were approved for elderly; 4. Most of those were also approved for children.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Approved for elderly → raised no one's BP. Contrapositive of fact 1: raised no one's BP → didn't reduce inflammation. So: approved for elderly → didn't reduce inflammation. Some elderly-approved drugs exist, and most of them were also approved for children. So at least one child-approved drug was elderly-approved and therefore didn't reduce inflammation. Watch out for drugs approved for children only; the facts say nothing about them.

choices.note: The trap. Drugs approved for children but not for the elderly are unconstrained. One of them could have reduced inflammation. 'None' is too strong.
The opposite. Every elderly-approved drug did NOT reduce inflammation, since reducing inflammation means raising someone's BP. This must be false.
Unsupported. Raising no one's BP is necessary for elderly approval, not sufficient. Most such drugs could have gone unapproved.

CORRECT. Elderly-approved → no BP rise → didn't reduce inflammation. Some elderly-approved drugs exist, and most of them were approved for children too, so at least one child-approved drug didn't reduce inflammation.
Not guaranteed. Fact 1 only kicks in if a drug reduced inflammation. Maybe no drug did, and maybe none raised BP. Then this would be false.

questions.stimulus: Manager: Last year our firm began allowing employees in its design department to work from home two days a week. Since then, the number of projects the design department completes each month has risen by 15 percent. Clearly, allowing employees to work from home increases their productivity, so we should extend the policy to every department in the firm.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager’s argument?
choices: A few employees in the design department chose not to work from home even after the policy took effect.
Shortly after the policy took effect, the design department hired four additional designers, enlarging its staff by 20 percent.
Employees in several of the firm’s other departments have said that they would like to work from home.
The projects completed by the design department last year were, on average, no smaller than those completed the year before.
Some of the firm’s managers believe that remote work makes employees more difficult to supervise.
questions.explanation: If the department’s staff grew by 20 percent while output grew by only 15 percent, output per employee actually fell, so the rise in completed projects does not show that remote work boosted productivity (B). D rules out an alternative explanation and so slightly strengthens the argument. A and E have little bearing on whether the policy raised productivity.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Working from home increases productivity, so the policy should be extended to every department.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the design department started allowing two remote days a week, its monthly completed projects rose 15%.

breakdown.analysis: Productivity means output per person, but the evidence is total output. If the department got bigger, total output could rise even while each person does less. It's like saying a restaurant's new music made cooks faster because it served more meals, when it also hired more cooks. Prephrase: something else, like more staff, explains the extra projects.

choices.note: A few people opting out doesn't matter. Most still worked from home, and output still went up. Barely relevant.
CORRECT. Staff grew 20% but output grew only 15%. So output per employee actually fell. The rise in projects shows nothing about remote work boosting productivity; it might have hurt it.
What other employees want has nothing to do with whether the policy raised productivity.
Slightly strengthens. It rules out the explanation that projects got smaller and so easier to finish. That helps the manager.
Some managers' opinions about supervision don't tell us whether productivity actually rose. Irrelevant to the evidence.

questions.stimulus: Legislator: The proposed tax credit for residential rooftop solar panels will reduce our state’s reliance on coal-fired power. The credit will lead many homeowners to install solar panels, and the electricity those panels generate will replace electricity the homeowners would otherwise have drawn from the power grid. At present, coal-fired plants supply the majority of the electricity on our state’s grid.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the legislator’s argument depends?
choices: Most homeowners who install solar panels after the credit takes effect would not have installed them without it.
Electricity from rooftop solar panels is less expensive to produce than electricity from coal-fired plants.
The tax credit will not significantly reduce the revenue available to the state government.
Coal-fired plants will continue to supply the majority of the electricity on the state’s grid for at least the next decade.
A reduction in the demand for electricity from the grid would lead to at least some reduction in the output of coal-fired plants.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from less demand for grid power to less reliance on coal; if reduced demand were met entirely by cutting output from other sources, coal use would not fall, so E is required. A is too strong: the argument needs only that some homeowners install panels because of the credit. D is also not needed, since coal could lose its majority and still have its output reduced.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rooftop solar tax credit will reduce the state's reliance on coal-fired power.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The credit will lead many homeowners to install panels; that solar power replaces electricity they'd have drawn from the grid; coal supplies most of the grid's electricity.

breakdown.analysis: The argument jumps from 'less demand on the grid' to 'less coal.' But grid operators could meet lower demand by cutting gas, hydro, or something else, and leave the coal plants running full blast. The argument needs lower grid demand to cut at least some coal output. Prephrase: reducing grid demand will reduce coal output at least somewhat. Negate each answer and see if the argument falls.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument only needs some homeowners to install panels because of the credit. Negate it: fewer than half would have skipped panels without it. The credit still causes some installs, which is enough.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most homeowners who install solar panels after the credit takes effect would not have installed them without it.

choices.note: Cost doesn't matter. The argument is about replacing grid electricity, not about which is cheaper. Negate it: solar costs more. The panels still displace grid power.
choices.negation: Electricity from rooftop solar panels is not less expensive to produce than electricity from coal-fired plants.

choices.note: State revenue is irrelevant to whether coal use drops. Negate it and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: The tax credit will significantly reduce the revenue available to the state government.

choices.note: Not needed. Coal could lose its majority and still see its output reduced by lower demand. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Coal-fired plants will not continue to supply the majority of the state's grid electricity for at least the next decade.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: lower grid demand would lead to no reduction at all in coal output. Then the solar power just pushes out other sources, coal keeps running, and reliance on coal doesn't drop. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: A reduction in the demand for electricity from the grid would not lead to any reduction in the output of coal-fired plants.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the Fernhill Public Library eliminated the fines it had charged for overdue books. Since then, the percentage of borrowed books that are returned after their due date has increased slightly. Over the same period, however, the number of borrowed books that are never returned at all has dropped substantially, even though the library has not changed its other policies for recovering unreturned books.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many borrowers who used to keep overdue books indefinitely did so to avoid paying the large fines that had accumulated on them.
Other libraries in the region that have eliminated overdue fines have also seen an increase in late returns.
The Fernhill Public Library has hired additional staff to process returned books more quickly.
The number of people borrowing books from the Fernhill Public Library has increased since fines were eliminated.
The fines the library had charged for overdue books had generated a substantial portion of its revenue.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why eliminating fines would make lateness more common but permanent non-return less common. A explains it: fines had deterred people from ever returning badly overdue books, so removing them brought those books back late rather than never. B explains only the rise in late returns, and D would, if anything, increase both figures rather than explain why one fell.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: After Fernhill eliminated overdue fines, late returns rose slightly, but books never returned at all dropped substantially.

breakdown.analysis: Dropping fines seems to make people less careful, and late returns did go up. So why did never-returned books fall? We need something that explains why fines kept some books away forever. Prephrase: the fines themselves stopped people from returning badly overdue books. It's like a parking ticket that's so big you'd rather avoid the lot forever than pay it; drop the ticket and people come back.

choices.note: CORRECT. Big accumulated fines made people keep overdue books indefinitely to avoid paying. Remove the fines and those books come back, late but returned. That explains both: more late returns, fewer never-returned books.
Only explains half. It confirms late returns rise without fines, which isn't the puzzling part. It says nothing about why never-returned books fell.
Faster processing doesn't make people bring books back. It doesn't explain why permanent non-returns dropped.
More borrowers would, if anything, increase both late returns and lost books. It doesn't explain why one number fell.
Revenue is irrelevant to borrower behavior. Doesn't touch either half of the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Some physicians have warned patients with high blood pressure to avoid the cold remedy Brevane. This warning, however, is unwarranted. Brevane contains three active ingredients, and in controlled studies each of them, taken alone at the dose found in Brevane, produced no measurable rise in blood pressure, even among patients whose blood pressure was poorly controlled. Since Brevane consists of nothing more than these three ingredients plus inert fillers, it too poses no risk to such patients.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the pharmacist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: rejects the physicians’ warning on the basis of their presumed motives rather than its merits
generalizes to all patients with high blood pressure from studies of patients whose blood pressure was poorly controlled
presumes that because each component of a product is harmless when taken in isolation, the product as a whole is harmless
overlooks the possibility that the fillers in Brevane, though inert, could themselves raise blood pressure
mistakes a factor that is merely associated with high blood pressure for a cause of it
questions.explanation: Each ingredient was tested only alone; the ingredients might interact to raise blood pressure when combined, so what holds of each part need not hold of the whole (C). B is the main trap, but studying patients with poorly controlled blood pressure makes the evidence stronger rather than weaker for other patients. D contradicts a premise the argument states, namely that the fillers are inert.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Physicians' warnings that high-blood-pressure patients avoid Brevane are unwarranted; it poses no risk to them.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each of Brevane's three active ingredients, taken alone at Brevane's dose, produced no measurable BP rise, even in poorly controlled patients; Brevane is just those three plus inert fillers.

breakdown.analysis: Each part is safe alone, so the whole is safe? Not necessarily. The ingredients could interact when combined. Part-to-whole flaw. It's like saying bleach is fine for cleaning and ammonia is fine for cleaning, so mixing them is fine for cleaning. Prephrase: assumes what's true of each ingredient alone is true of the combination.

choices.note: No attack on motives. The pharmacist argues from study data, not from what the physicians want.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The physicians' warning is unwarranted; they just want patients to buy pricier brand-name remedies.

choices.note: The main trap. Testing on patients with poorly controlled BP is the hardest case, so it makes the evidence stronger for other patients, not weaker. That's not a bad generalization.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A drug was safe for healthy young adults in trials, so it's safe for all patients, including those with heart disease.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each ingredient was tested only by itself. Brevane combines all three. The pharmacist assumes harmless parts make a harmless whole, ignoring that the ingredients might interact.
Contradicts a premise. The argument states the fillers are inert. On the LSAT, you accept premises; ignoring a possibility the argument already ruled out isn't a flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This cake is safe for my nut-allergic friend because the flour, sugar and eggs are nut-free; I never checked the frosting.

choices.note: There's no correlation mistaken for causation here. The argument is about whether something causes a BP rise, and its evidence is controlled studies.
choices.example: Example of flaw: People with high blood pressure tend to drink a lot of coffee, so coffee must cause high blood pressure.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A manager should publicly credit an individual employee for a team’s success only if that employee’s contribution was both essential to the success and substantially greater than that of any other member of the team.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Okafor acted properly in publicly crediting Lin for the success of the product launch, since Lin’s work was essential to it, even though two other team members contributed just as much.
Hale acted improperly in failing to publicly credit Marsh for the success of the audit, since Marsh’s contribution was essential and far exceeded that of any other team member.

Brandt acted properly in publicly crediting Yusuf for the success of the merger, since Yusuf contributed far more than anyone else, even though the merger would have succeeded without that contribution.
Ruiz acted improperly in publicly crediting Dalton for the success of the campaign, since although Dalton’s work was indispensable, Pereira’s contribution was equally large.
Singh acted improperly in publicly crediting the entire team, rather than any single member, for the success of the redesign.
questions.explanation: The principle states two necessary conditions for crediting an individual; in D, Dalton’s contribution was not greater than Pereira’s, so crediting Dalton violated the principle and the judgment of impropriety conforms. B is the trap: the principle gives only necessary conditions for crediting someone, so it never requires crediting anyone and cannot show Hale acted improperly. A and C approve credit when one of the conditions fails, and E concerns team credit, which the principle does not address.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Manager publicly credits an individual for team success → that employee's contribution was essential AND substantially greater than any other member's. Contrapositive: not essential OR not substantially greater → don't credit that individual.

breakdown.analysis: 'Only if' gives necessary conditions. The rule can tell you when crediting someone is wrong (a condition is missing). It can never tell you that you must credit someone, because meeting the necessary conditions doesn't trigger any requirement. So look for a judgment saying a manager acted improperly by crediting someone who failed a condition.

choices.note: Fails the second condition. Two others contributed just as much, so Lin's contribution wasn't substantially greater than everyone else's. The rule says crediting Lin was improper, not proper.

The trap. Marsh meets both conditions, but the rule only lists requirements for crediting someone. It never says you must credit anyone who meets them. So it can't show Hale acted improperly by staying quiet.
Fails the first condition. The merger would have succeeded without Yusuf, so his contribution wasn't essential. The rule says crediting him was improper, not proper.

CORRECT. Dalton's work was essential, but Pereira's was equally large, so Dalton's wasn't substantially greater than everyone else's. Missing condition → shouldn't credit him. So Ruiz acted improperly. Matches the rule.
The rule is about crediting individuals. It says nothing about crediting the whole team, so it can't support calling that improper.

questions.stimulus: In the Marrow Basin, fog forms only on nights when the ground cools enough that the air just above it reaches its dew point, the temperature at which water vapor condenses. Cloud cover at night slows the cooling of the ground by trapping heat radiated from the surface. Over the past twenty years, the average amount of nighttime cloud cover over the basin has increased substantially, while the average humidity of the basin’s air has remained essentially unchanged.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Over the past twenty years, nights on which fog forms in the Marrow Basin have probably become less frequent.
Fog never forms in the Marrow Basin on nights when there is substantial cloud cover.
The humidity of the air is the most important factor in determining whether fog forms in the Marrow Basin.
The increase in nighttime cloud cover over the Marrow Basin has been caused by changes in the region’s climate.
Days following foggy nights in the Marrow Basin tend to be cooler than days following clear nights.
questions.explanation: More cloud cover means the ground cools less at night, and with humidity unchanged, the air will reach its dew point less often, so fog has probably become less frequent (A). B is too strong, since clouds only slow cooling and do not prevent it. C and D make claims about relative importance and about causes that the passage does not address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Fog forms → ground cools enough for air to reach dew point; 2. Night cloud cover slows ground cooling by trapping heat; 3. Over 20 years, nighttime cloud cover increased substantially; 4. Average humidity stayed essentially the same.

breakdown.analysis: More clouds → less ground cooling → the air reaches its dew point less often. And since humidity hasn't changed, the dew point hasn't shifted to make up for it. So fog should be forming less often. Prephrase: fog nights have probably become less frequent. Keep it modest: the passage supports a 'probably,' not a 'never.'

choices.note: CORRECT. More cloud cover means slower cooling, so fewer nights reach the dew point, with humidity holding steady. Fog has probably become less common. 'Probably' fits the evidence.
Too strong. Clouds slow cooling; they don't stop it. The ground might still cool enough on some cloudy nights. 'Never' isn't supported.
Ranking claim the passage doesn't make. It says nothing about humidity being more important than cooling or anything else.
The passage doesn't say why cloud cover increased. Cause of the clouds is unaddressed.
Daytime temperatures after fog aren't discussed at all.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Every poem in Halloran’s new collection, except the prose poems, relies heavily on enjambment, the running of a sentence past the end of a line without a pause. Any poem that relies heavily on enjambment loses much of its effect when read aloud, because listeners cannot hear where the lines end. And each of the collection’s prose poems runs longer than ten pages. It follows that none of the poems in Halloran’s new collection is suitable for a public reading.
questions.stem: The critic’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any poem that loses much of its effect when read aloud is unsuitable for a public reading.
A poem is suitable for a public reading if it neither loses much of its effect when read aloud nor runs longer than ten pages.
No prose poem that runs longer than ten pages relies heavily on enjambment.
Most poems that run longer than ten pages lose much of their effect when read aloud.
A poem is suitable for a public reading only if it does not lose much of its effect when read aloud and does not run longer than ten pages.
questions.explanation: E says that losing effect aloud or running over ten pages each rules a poem out; the non-prose poems lose effect aloud and the prose poems run over ten pages, so every poem is ruled out. A is the trap: it rules out the enjambed poems but says nothing about the prose poems. B reverses the conditional, giving conditions for suitability rather than for unsuitability, and D is only a ‘most’ claim about length.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the poems in Halloran's new collection is suitable for a public reading.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every non-prose poem relies heavily on enjambment; heavy enjambment → loses much effect read aloud; every prose poem runs over ten pages.

breakdown.analysis: Two groups, and each needs its own path to 'unsuitable.' Non-prose poems → enjambment → lose effect aloud. Prose poems → over ten pages. We need: loses effect aloud → unsuitable, AND over ten pages → unsuitable. Equivalent: suitable → doesn't lose effect AND isn't over ten pages. Any answer that handles only one group leaves the other uncovered.

choices.note: The trap. It handles the enjambed poems (lose effect → unsuitable) but says nothing about the prose poems, which are covered only by length. Half a bridge.
Reversed. It gives conditions for being suitable, not for being unsuitable. Knowing what guarantees suitability says nothing about poems that fail those conditions.
Just tells us the prose poems don't use enjambment. Doesn't connect anything to suitability.
'Most' long poems lose effect, and even that doesn't link to suitability. Doesn't guarantee anything about Halloran's prose poems.

CORRECT. Suitable → doesn't lose effect AND isn't over ten pages. Contrapositive: loses effect OR over ten pages → unsuitable. Non-prose poems lose effect; prose poems run long. Every poem is ruled out.

questions.stimulus: Some researchers attribute the recent decline of the Ashby firefly to pesticide runoff from nearby farms. This explanation, however, is inadequate. The firefly has declined just as sharply within the Ashby nature reserve, where pesticides have been banned for decades, as on the surrounding farmland. A more likely culprit is artificial light. Ashby fireflies locate mates by means of their flashes, and both the reserve and the farmland have seen a dramatic increase in nighttime light from nearby housing developments over the same period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the firefly has declined just as sharply within the reserve as on the surrounding farmland?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is used to undermine a rival hypothesis by showing that the decline occurs even where the factor that hypothesis cites is absent.
It is a hypothesis that the argument considers and ultimately endorses.
It is presented as evidence that the factor the argument favors is at work in both the reserve and the farmland.
It is a claim that the argument concedes but maintains is irrelevant to its conclusion.
questions.explanation: The equal decline inside a reserve where pesticides are banned shows that the pesticide hypothesis, which the argument rejects, cannot account for the decline (B). D is the trap: the rise in nighttime light in both places is established by a separate, later claim, and the claim in question says nothing about light. The claim is a premise, not the main conclusion (A) or a hypothesis (C).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Artificial light, not pesticide runoff, is the more likely cause of the Ashby firefly's decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The firefly declined just as sharply in the reserve, where pesticides have been banned for decades, as on farmland; fireflies find mates by flashing; nighttime light rose in both areas.

breakdown.analysis: The claim in question is a premise aimed at the rival hypothesis. If pesticides were the cause, the reserve (no pesticides) should have fared better. It didn't. So pesticides can't explain the decline. It's like blaming a cough on a smoky kitchen, but you cough just as much when you're away from the kitchen. A separate claim, about lights, supports the author's own hypothesis.

choices.note: The main conclusion is that artificial light is the more likely culprit (and pesticides an inadequate explanation). This claim is evidence, not the point.
CORRECT. Equal decline in a pesticide-free reserve shows the decline happens even where the rival hypothesis's cause is absent. That undermines the pesticide explanation.
It's not a hypothesis; it's an observed fact. The hypothesis the argument endorses is that artificial light is responsible.
The trap. The rise of nighttime light in both places comes from a separate, later claim. The claim in question says nothing about light; it's about the decline being equal.
The argument doesn't call it irrelevant. It's central: it's what knocks out the pesticide hypothesis.

questions.stimulus: Economist: In Brayton, the new rule requiring that 15 percent of the units in large new apartment buildings be rented at below-market rates has caused a slowdown in residential construction. In the two years since the rule took effect, applications for permits to build large apartment buildings in Brayton have fallen by 40 percent compared with the two years before the rule took effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist’s argument?
choices: Several developers who build large apartment buildings in Brayton have publicly criticized the rule.
Permit applications for small apartment buildings, which are exempt from the rule, have increased in Brayton since the rule took effect.
The rule was announced well before it took effect, and developers rushed to file applications before the effective date so that their projects would be exempt.
Apartments rented at below-market rates in Brayton have long waiting lists of prospective tenants.
Large apartment buildings in Brayton typically take more than two years to complete once a permit application has been filed.
questions.explanation: C attacks the comparison rather than the conclusion: if developers rushed applications into the period just before the rule took effect, the baseline is inflated and much of the 40 percent drop reflects shifted timing rather than a real slowdown. B is a tempting trap but actually strengthens the argument, since unregulated building kept growing. E concerns completion time, which does not affect the count of applications filed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brayton's below-market-units rule caused a slowdown in residential construction.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In the two years since the rule took effect, permit applications for large apartment buildings fell 40% compared with the two years before.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after comparisons depend on the 'before' being normal. If developers knew the rule was coming and rushed to file early, the 'before' period is inflated and the 'after' period is drained, because projects that would have been filed later got pulled forward. The drop could be mostly a timing shift, not a real slowdown. It's like a store seeing a huge drop in sales the week after a big pre-announced price hike: everyone stocked up the week before.

choices.note: Developers complaining doesn't show the rule didn't cause the drop. If anything, it fits the economist's story.
Tempting, but it actually strengthens. Exempt small buildings kept growing while covered large buildings fell. That points to the rule as the difference.

CORRECT. Developers rushed applications in before the rule took effect. That inflates the 'before' count and pulls projects out of the 'after' period. Much of the 40% drop could be shifted timing, not a real slowdown.
Waiting lists for below-market units say nothing about whether the rule slowed construction.
Completion time doesn't affect how many permit applications were filed. The evidence is about applications, so this misses the target.

questions.stimulus: Archivist: Some people argue that because digital scans make the contents of fragile manuscripts widely accessible, libraries no longer need to devote resources to preserving the original documents. But if this reasoning were sound, then the existence of detailed photographs of a historic building would mean that there was no need to preserve the building itself. No one would accept that conclusion, since a building, like a manuscript, contains information about its materials, its construction, and its history of use that no image can fully capture.
questions.stem: The archivist’s argument proceeds by
choices: questioning the motives of those who advance the view being criticized
offering evidence that digital scans of manuscripts are frequently inaccurate
presenting a single counterexample to a generalization about all manuscripts
showing that similar reasoning, applied to an analogous case, would lead to an unacceptable conclusion
demonstrating that the opposing view’s conclusion contradicts one of its own premises
questions.explanation: The archivist applies the opponents’ reasoning to buildings and photographs, notes that the resulting conclusion is clearly unacceptable, and so rejects the original reasoning (D). C is tempting, but the building case is an analogy, not a manuscript that contradicts a generalization. The archivist never claims scans are inaccurate (B) or discusses motives (A).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reasoning that digital scans make preserving original manuscripts unnecessary is unsound (implied).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By the same logic, detailed photos would make preserving historic buildings unnecessary; no one accepts that, because buildings, like manuscripts, hold information images can't capture.

breakdown.analysis: This is argument by parallel reasoning: take the opponent's logic, apply it to a similar case, and show it produces something absurd. If the logic gives a ridiculous answer there, it can't be trusted here. It's like answering 'we have the recipe, so we don't need the chef' with 'by that logic, we have sheet music, so we don't need musicians.'

choices.note: No talk of motives. The archivist goes after the reasoning itself.
choices.example: Example of method: Those who say we don't need originals are just trying to cut the library's budget so they can fund their own projects.

choices.note: The archivist never says scans are inaccurate. The point is that even perfect images miss things like materials and construction.
choices.example: Example of method: A study found that 30% of digital scans contain errors, so scans can't replace originals.

choices.note: Tempting, but the building is an analogy, not a counterexample. A counterexample would be a specific manuscript that breaks a general claim about manuscripts.
choices.example: Example of method: Some say all medieval manuscripts are on vellum, but the Harlow Psalter is on paper.

choices.note: CORRECT. The archivist applies the same reasoning (an image makes the original unnecessary) to buildings and photographs, notes that the result is unacceptable, and so rejects the reasoning.
The archivist doesn't show the opponents contradict themselves. The problem shown is that their reasoning leads somewhere absurd in a similar case.
choices.example: Example of method: They say originals don't matter, yet they also say the original is the only reliable source for scans. Those claims can't both be true.

questions.stimulus: Every house in the Ostrand historic district that was built before 1920 has a slate roof, unless it was substantially rebuilt after a fire. The Whitcomb house stands in the Ostrand district and does not have a slate roof, but it has never been substantially rebuilt after a fire. Therefore, the Whitcomb house was not built before 1920.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every painting in the Harrow collection that was acquired before 1900 has been restored, unless it is on long-term loan. The portrait of Ada Venn is in the Harrow collection and has not been restored. Therefore, it was not acquired before 1900.

Every tenor in the Greenleaf choir attends the Thursday rehearsal, unless excused by the director. Paulo, a member of the choir, attends the Thursday rehearsal and has not been excused. Therefore, Paulo sings tenor.

Every bridge in Dunmore County that was built before 1950 has been inspected this year, unless it is closed to traffic. The Mill Road bridge is in Dunmore County and has not been inspected this year. Therefore, it either was not built before 1950 or is closed to traffic.

No vehicle in the city fleet that runs on diesel is more than ten years old, unless it has been overhauled. The street sweeper is in the fleet, is more than ten years old, and has been overhauled. Therefore, it runs on diesel.

Every restaurant on Cole Street that opened last year serves breakfast, unless it lacks a full kitchen. The Bluebird Café is on Cole Street and does not serve breakfast, but it has a full kitchen. Therefore, the Bluebird Café did not open last year.
questions.explanation: The original: every member of a group with feature X has feature Y unless exception Z; this member lacks Y and lacks Z; so it lacks X. E matches every element. A is the main trap but never rules out the exception (the loan), so its conclusion does not follow. C is valid but never eliminates the exception, so it reaches a disjunctive conclusion instead; B and D reverse the logic.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Whitcomb house was not built before 1920.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ostrand house built before 1920 → slate roof, unless substantially rebuilt after a fire; Whitcomb is in Ostrand, has no slate roof, and was never rebuilt after a fire.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Every X in the group has Y unless Z; this one lacks Y and lacks Z; so it isn't X. (Valid.)

breakdown.analysis: Turn 'unless' into arrows. Built before 1920 AND not rebuilt → slate roof. Contrapositive: no slate roof → not built before 1920 OR rebuilt. Whitcomb wasn't rebuilt, so it wasn't built before 1920. Valid. The matching answer must (1) state the same 'unless' rule, (2) show the subject lacks the result, (3) rule out the exception, and (4) conclude the subject lacks the first feature.

choices.note: The main trap. Same rule shape, and Ada Venn hasn't been restored, but the argument never rules out the exception: she might be on long-term loan. Without that, the conclusion doesn't follow.
Reversed. Tenor → attends, unless excused. Paulo attends, so he's a tenor? That's affirming the result. Lots of non-tenors might attend too. Invalid.
Valid, but different. It never eliminates the exception, so it concludes 'either not built before 1950 or closed.' The original rules out the exception and lands on a single conclusion.
Reversed and flawed. Diesel → not over ten years, unless overhauled. The sweeper is old and overhauled, so it runs on diesel? Being overhauled doesn't prove it's diesel. Invalid.

CORRECT. Opened last year → serves breakfast, unless no full kitchen. Bluebird doesn't serve breakfast but has a full kitchen (exception ruled out). So it didn't open last year. Every piece matches, right down to the 'but.'

questions.stimulus: Utility spokesperson: Critics of the proposed Grisham Ridge wind farm claim that it will force the utility to raise its electricity rates. But under state regulations, the utility may raise its rates only if its operating costs increase, and the wind farm will reduce those costs. After all, wind turbines require no fuel, and fuel purchases are by far the largest component of the utility’s current operating costs. So the critics’ claim is mistaken.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the spokesperson’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that savings in one component of a total will not be offset by increases in its other components
treats a condition that is necessary for the utility to raise its rates as though it were sufficient
rejects the critics’ claim on the basis of the critics’ presumed motives rather than its merits
fails to consider that the state might revise its regulations governing electricity rates
assumes that fuel purchases will remain the largest component of the utility’s costs after the wind farm is built
questions.explanation: Cutting fuel purchases reduces operating costs only if the wind farm does not add other operating costs, such as maintenance and transmission, that exceed the fuel savings (A). B is the trap: the argument uses the regulation correctly, moving from costs not increasing to rates not rising, which is a valid contrapositive. E is not needed, since fuel can lose its top ranking and the argument is unaffected.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics are wrong that the wind farm will force the utility to raise rates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Utility may raise rates → operating costs increase; the wind farm will reduce operating costs, because turbines need no fuel and fuel is the biggest cost component.

breakdown.analysis: The regulation part is fine: costs don't rise → no rate hike. The weak spot is 'the wind farm will reduce costs.' Saving on fuel cuts one line on the bill, but the wind farm could add others: maintenance, transmission lines, staff, debt payments. If those add up to more than the fuel savings, total costs go up. It's like saying switching to an electric car will cut my driving costs because I'll buy no gas, without asking about the car payment and the charging bill.

choices.note: CORRECT. Fuel savings cut one component of operating costs. The argument assumes nothing else goes up enough to offset that, like turbine maintenance or transmission. That's the gap.
The trap. The argument uses the regulation correctly. Rates rise → costs increase. Contrapositive: costs don't increase → rates don't rise. That's valid, not a necessary-sufficient mix-up.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The utility can raise rates only if costs go up. Costs went up, so the utility will raise rates.

choices.note: The spokesperson doesn't attack the critics' motives; it's all about costs and regulations.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics only oppose the wind farm because it would spoil the view from their vacation homes, so their claim about rates is wrong.

choices.note: The argument is about the current rules. Possible future changes are a stretch, not the core weakness.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Under current law, stores can't open on Sundays, so the new mall will never open on a Sunday.

choices.note: Not needed. Even if fuel stops being the biggest cost, the argument only needs total costs not to rise. A ranking change doesn't break it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Rent is our biggest expense, so as long as we cut rent, rent will stay our biggest expense and our costs will fall.

questions.stimulus: Researchers gave patients who suffer from chronic migraines either the drug Tolvarin or a placebo for six months. Patients receiving Tolvarin reported 40 percent fewer migraines than those receiving the placebo. Tolvarin, however, produces a distinctive metallic taste that most patients notice within a few days. Nevertheless, the researchers conclude that Tolvarin reduces the frequency of migraines through its pharmacological action and not merely through patients’ expectations about the drug.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers’ argument?
choices: Most patients in the Tolvarin group correctly guessed, partway through the study, that they were receiving the drug.
In an earlier study using a taste-masked form of Tolvarin, patients reported fewer migraines after six months than before treatment began.
Patients in the Tolvarin group who never noticed the metallic taste reported reductions in migraines as large as those reported by patients who noticed it.
The metallic taste produced by Tolvarin fades for most patients after the first few weeks of treatment.
Tolvarin is chemically similar to a drug that is widely used to lower blood pressure.
questions.explanation: The worry is that the taste tipped patients off and their expectations, not the drug, reduced the migraines. Patients who never noticed the taste had no such cue, so their equal improvement points to the drug itself (C). B is the most tempting trap, but without a placebo comparison a before-and-after improvement could reflect expectation or natural variation. D does not help, because expectations formed in the early weeks could persist after the taste fades, and A weakens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tolvarin reduces migraines through its pharmacological action, not just through patients' expectations.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tolvarin patients reported 40% fewer migraines than placebo patients over six months; but Tolvarin has a distinctive metallic taste most patients notice within days.

breakdown.analysis: The taste breaks the blind. Patients who notice it can guess they're on the real drug, and that expectation alone might reduce migraines. To strengthen, find patients who got the drug but had no clue, and show they improved just as much. It's like testing whether a new coffee really wakes you up: give some people the coffee without telling them, and see whether they perk up as much as the people who knew.

choices.note: Weakens. If most Tolvarin patients figured out they were on the drug, expectation becomes an even more plausible explanation.
The most tempting trap. Taste-masking removes the cue, but there's no placebo group. A before-and-after improvement could come from expectation of being treated, or natural ups and downs.
CORRECT. Patients who never noticed the taste had no cue that they were on the drug, yet they improved just as much as those who noticed. That isolates the drug's own effect from expectations.
Doesn't help. Expectations formed in the first few weeks can stick around after the taste fades. The blind was already broken.
Chemical similarity to a blood-pressure drug says nothing about whether Tolvarin works on migraines through its chemistry or through expectation.

questions.stimulus: Consultant: At Pelham Logistics, warehouse teams whose members hold a brief meeting at the start of each shift have markedly lower error rates than teams that skip such meetings. Currently, about half of Pelham’s warehouse teams hold these meetings voluntarily. Therefore, if Pelham’s management requires every warehouse team to hold a start-of-shift meeting, the company’s overall warehouse error rate will decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the consultant’s argument?
choices: Teams that hold start-of-shift meetings have lower error rates than other teams on every type of warehouse task.
Start-of-shift meetings would reduce errors at least somewhat even among teams that hold them only because they are required to.
The lower error rates of teams that hold start-of-shift meetings are due entirely to the meetings and not to any other difference between those teams and the rest.
Start-of-shift meetings are the most effective means available to Pelham for reducing warehouse errors.
Pelham’s overall warehouse error rate is higher than that of comparable logistics companies.
questions.explanation: The teams that would newly hold meetings would do so only under compulsion; if meetings held that way did nothing, the overall rate would not fall, so B is required. C is the strongest trap: the argument needs the meetings to account for some of the difference, not all of it, so ‘entirely’ makes C stronger than necessary. A and D are likewise more than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If Pelham requires every warehouse team to hold start-of-shift meetings, the overall error rate will decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Teams that hold start-of-shift meetings have much lower error rates than teams that skip them; about half the teams currently hold them voluntarily.

breakdown.analysis: The teams that currently meet chose to. The teams that will newly meet are being forced. Maybe meetings only help when people want them, and a forced meeting is just ten minutes of eye-rolling. The argument needs the meetings to do at least some good for teams that hold them only because they're required. It's like assuming that because kids who choose to practice piano play well, making every kid practice will help. Negate each answer to find the one that breaks the argument.

choices.note: Too strong. The overall rate can drop even if meetings don't help on every single task type. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: On some type of warehouse task, teams that hold start-of-shift meetings do not have lower error rates than other teams.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: required meetings wouldn't reduce errors at all among teams that hold them only because they must. Then the newly meeting teams don't improve, the voluntary teams were already meeting, and the overall rate doesn't fall. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Start-of-shift meetings would not reduce errors at all among teams that hold them only because they are required to.

choices.note: The strongest trap. The argument needs the meetings to cause some of the difference, not all of it. Negate it: some of the gap comes from other differences between teams. Meetings could still cause part of it, and the overall rate could still drop.
choices.negation: The lower error rates of teams that hold start-of-shift meetings are due at least partly to some difference other than the meetings.

choices.note: Not needed. The argument says the rate will decline, not that meetings are the best tool. Negate it: there's a better method. Meetings could still help.
choices.negation: Start-of-shift meetings are not the most effective means available to Pelham for reducing warehouse errors.

choices.note: Comparing to other companies is irrelevant. Negate it: Pelham's rate is already lower than competitors'. It could still decline further.
